speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: MR. POULIOT    FELICITATIONS ON ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at the moment on a question not so much of privilege as of courtesy. Yesterday afternoon I happened to look through the Parliamentary Guide, and found that one of our distinguished members in the house is today celebrating his twenty-eighth anniversary as a member of the house. I refer of course to our genial and very good friend, the hon. member for Temiscouata, Mr. Jean Frangois Pouliot.
He was first elected to the House of Commons in a by-election on December 1, 1924, and has been elected in seven general elections since that time, a period of twenty-eight years-three years more than a quarter of a century.
While in the house we may have our differences, while there may be harsh words exchanged at different times across the floor of the chamber, nevertheless I think that on an occasion of this kind we might pause a moment and pay a well-deserved mark of courtesy to one of our senior members in the house. I do this with a great deal of pleasure, although perhaps all too inadequately.
I noticed further, in reviewing the comments in the Parliamentary Guide, that the Pouliot family has been quite distinguished in its record of public service. I believe the hon. member's father was a member of the House of Commons, and that his grandfather and great-grandfather served in various legislative capacities.
It is clear therefore that the background of the Pouliot family in the public life of this country has been most significant. Having in mind the atmosphere of this institution, and what it means to serve here a long time, I think all hon. members this afternoon would wish to pay our tribute of respect, and to offer our congratulations and very best wishes to the hon. member for Temiscouata.
I believe I speak for all members in the House of Commons when I extend to the hon. member our very best wishes.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
maintopic: MR. POULIOT    FELICITATIONS ON ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I indicate my own hope that everyone will join in extending good wishes to the very genial member for Temiscouata. May I point out that he occupies a unique position in the house, not only by reason of the association of his family with the public service of this country, but perhaps in another way. I refer of course to the fact that he has differences of opinion not only across the floor of the house, but at times even on the same side of the house. In the relatively short time I have been here, he has never hesitated in that respect to express his opinion. He knows I do not always share his opinions, and I have discovered he does not always share mine. I know that with whatever friendship I extend my congratulations today, and I do so with good friendship indeed, he will not expect me to assist him unduly in continuing this long record of public service-although I must say he seems to have got on very well without that in the past.
In all seriousness may I say that it is a matter for comment that in one family there should be such a unique record of public service. When anyone can look back on 28 years of personal service and recall that his father, his grandfather and his great-grandfather served Canada in a similar capacity, it is indeed right that he should claim to have sought to help Canada by serving the country publicly. In doing so there has been established a family tradition.
Whatever differences of opinion there may be, and these differences of opinion characterize this free democratic system of ours, may I add to what has been said already-I feel sure that this is the conviction of every hon. member here-and extend to the hon. member for Temiscouata all good wishes and hopes that he may enjoy in health and happiness the many friendships he has established.

maintopic: MR. POULIOT    FELICITATIONS ON ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the official whip of the government and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) have spoken for all of us. In the seventeen years that I have been here it has been my pleasure to sit almost directly opposite to the hon. member for Temiscouata. Not only have I listened to his contributions to the debates that have appeared in Hansard; I have also heard the witticisms in which he has indulged and which on occasion did not

Felicitations to Mr. Pouliot
get into Hansard. I have enjoyed both and I hope that at least for the lifetime of this parliament all of us may continue to enjoy these witticisms.
As the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir) have said, it is unique that a dynasty in elective service, for such it is, should have been established in parliament and legislatures for four generations. I would hope that this tradition will be carried on when the time comes by the young son of the hon. member. I am very happy indeed to join in these felicitations.

maintopic: MR. POULIOT    FELICITATIONS ON ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is obvious to all present that there is nothing further to be said. The Social Credit group join with their fellow members in the fine things that have been said concerning the hon. member for Temiscouata.

maintopic: MR. POULIOT    FELICITATIONS ON ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as next-door neighbour to the hon. member for Temiscouata in our room accommodations, and as a friend of long standing, I want to say a word about the hon. member. For a short period of time I occupied the position of leader of the opposition, and at that time I am afraid I was a very green stick of political timber. While I was carrying on my duties in that capacity, I shall never forget the great kindness and the extreme courtesy that I always received from the experienced and brilliant member for Temiscouata.
At all times I have been the recipient of many acts of kindness, in and out of the house, by this member from the province of Quebec. Two years ago he came into the county of Peel to address one of our important organizations which, I hasten to say, has nothing to do with politics. I think he left one of the best impressions that any parliamentarian who has come into my part of the country has ever left upon the people. As an ambassador of good will between the different sections of Canada he has made an outstanding success.
Quite often at the United Nations-I am sure my feelings are shared by other members who have been there-when listening to Vishinsky carrying on in his top form and doing the most damage he could, I have wished that for a few fleeting minutes Jean Frangois Pouliot could be there to deal with him as he deserved.
When he visited us in Brampton two years ago we presented his charming wife, through him, with a bouquet of flowers from the flower town of Canada. I only wanted to rise and add to that bouquet a verbal orchid of my own.
[Mr. Coldwell.l

maintopic: MR. POULIOT    FELICITATIONS ON ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a former deskmate of the hon. member for Temiscouata, may I say that I have always found him courteous and kind to me in my inexperience, and sober, sensible and convincing in his remarks. I want to bring to him greetings from a number of friends in Fort William who wish him at least 28 years more in the House of Commons. We wish him not only success here but peace in his own heart.

maintopic: MR. POULIOT    FELICITATIONS ON ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the chief government whip, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), the hon. gentleman who leads the C.C.F. group (Mr. Coldwell), the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), my good friend the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), and my good friend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor).
I am quite fortunate in having been a member of parliament for 28 years. I went through eight general elections, three within twenty-two months, and here I am listening to the finest obituary to which one could listen. It was most kind of the whip to speak as he did and I am deeply touched by what he and the other gentlemen said.
I remember when I was first elected to the House of Commons 28 years ago. It was a Monday like today, with fine weather. It had been a terrific election. When I was invited to the land of flowers, to Brampton, to speak before a social club there, I told them some of the incidents that had occurred during that election and perhaps I could repeat one or two at this time.
I did not run as an independent, I ran as a straight Liberal. The official candidate was not actually the member for Temiscouata, it was another gentleman. It was quite difficult to convince some of the diehard Liberals that their duty was to vote for me. Therefore my friends got a good-looking chap with dark hair who went from house to house to canvass the people. He told them that he was Mackenzie King's messenger and that it was their duty to vote for Pouliot. When they asked his name he said he was Chubby Power. He was not actually the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), he was just a good friend of mine. There was no impersonation, because he voted in his own name. That is just one of the numerous stories I told in Brampton.
I think my hon. friends know that I do not intend to make a long speech but I would like to tell the house the secret for survival in politics. I think each member of parliament knows it. The motto we used to read

in our copy books when we were at school- "Honesty is the best policy". Another one is "I serve."

maintopic: MR. POULIOT    FELICITATIONS ON ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Is that illustrated by the story?

maintopic: MR. POULIOT    FELICITATIONS ON ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
One must stand by one's own people provided that the member honestly believes they are right; and if they are wrong, which happens seldom, he must tell them so. This is the only condition for survival. Besides that one must not promise more than can be done.
I never expected that so many members of parliament would be so kind. I have done my best to be fair with all my colleagues without distinction, and if we disagree at times with regard to various policies we nevertheless have a common bond that ties us very strongly, namely, that though we may belong to this or that party we are in the first place members of the House of Commons and as such we are brothers. Not only that, I think that the members of the House of Commons form indeed an exclusive club. They also form a very representative crosssection of the country and a very good slice of mankind. Those who come here to attend our deliberations are in a position to have a fair opinion of the Canadian people at large.
I have been touched iby the very kind remarks of all those who have spoken, by the remarks of the whip who has always been very kind to me. Often when I was not sure what to do I sought advice from him, and he has been most helpful to me, as have all my colleagues. I have also appreciated warmly the kind words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). We disagree but we remain friends. This is a thing that is essential in public life; otherwise life would be unbearable. I say the same thing of the leader of the C.C.F. group and the former leader of the Social Credit party. They have been very generous to me. I appreciate it. I do not know what are the future plans of my son. I do not think he will get into politics but I will surely send him a copy of Hansard.
It was very kind of my good neighbour, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), who was formerly leader of the opposition, to associate the name of my wife with the work that I have done as a member of parliament. Our wives deserve even more sympathy than we who are in politics. Life is very hard for them, and I have been comforted by the kindness and the support of my wife. I am very thankful to her and I am thankful to my electors who have been most kind to me. They have been fair, they have been very generous and kind to me, and I cannot speak highly enough of them. I managed well with my neighbour.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INVESTIGATION OF PLANES OVER CANADIAN TERRITORY BY UNITED STATES AIRCRAFT
speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of National Defence. Under what authority do United States planes cross into Canada for the purpose of investigating planes flying over Canadian territory?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INVESTIGATION OF PLANES OVER CANADIAN TERRITORY BY UNITED STATES AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
As hon. members know, the defence of North America must be regarded as a single operation, and in consequence of recommendations of the permanent joint board an arrangement has been worked out related to the defence of North America against air attack. The important element in this arrangement is that air defence identification zones have been set up along both sides of the international border and along both coasts. Civil aeronautical regulations require that any aircraft operating in these zones should file flight plans.

Inquiries of the Ministry
Any unidentified aircraft flying in an air defence zone near the international border and apparently heading toward the border is liable to interception for purposes of identification by military aircraft of the country towards which the unidentified aircraft is believed to be headed. For this purpose United States air force aircraft may cross the border into Canada and R.C.A.F. aircraft may cross into the United States. Interceptor aircraft must obey the rules of interception procedure laid down by the country over which the interception is made. United States aircraft when flying over Canada are not permitted to order any aircraft to land.
With respect to the press report which gives rise to this matter, I think I should say that the Globe and Mail refers to three specific incidents. The information made available to me by officers of the R.C.A.F. and by the Department of Transport would indicate that one incident referred to as taking place recently and involving a Leavens Brothers aircraft actually took place in 1950 long before this arrangement was in effect. Another incident referred to concerned an Austin Airways plane. This, I am informed, related to an incident that occurred well on the United States side of the border. I am informed that no report regarding the interception of the Ed Thomas-piloted photographic plane has been received by either air force headquarters or the Department of Transport, but from their own information they believe it occurred in March or April of 1952.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INTEGRATION OF SOUTH KOREAN FORCES WITH CANADIAN UNITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) a question? Recent reports would indicate that there is a new policy being followed with regard to the integration of South Korean troops with Canadian units. Could the minister indicate whether the reports are or are not correct?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxion (Minisier of National Defence):
maintopic: INTEGRATION OF SOUTH KOREAN FORCES WITH CANADIAN UNITS
speechtext:
It is the policy of the Canadian government to support any action which will enhance the military effectiveness of the South Koreans and to assist them to defend their own country. On a proposal emanating from commonwealth representatives with the United Nations command, discussions have taken place with other commonwealth countries concerned, with a view to reaching agreement on the integration of South Korean personnel into units of the first commonwealth division.
For some months past the United States divisions in Korea have integrated a number of South Koreans divided among their division units. The American practice has been to feed, clothe and lend arms to the South Koreans serving with United States units, while the South Korean government has been responsible for their pay. It is probable that the arrangements contemplated for the integration of South Koreans into the commonwealth division, if agreed to, will be on lines similar in effect to the United States formations.

maintopic: FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE STATEMENT BY UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE STATEMENT BY UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
With permission of the house I should like to place on record a statement which was issued from Washington the other day and forwarded to us. It was issued on November 28 and reads as follows:
Acting Secretary of Agriculture Knox T. Hutchinson announced today that if present favourable conditions continue, Canada will be declared free of foot-and-mouth disease on March 1, 1953.
Consultations were held with the department's livestock industry advisory committee on foot and mouth disease in Denver this week regarding the re-opening of the Canadian border to livestock and livestock products. The committee recommended the March 1 date.
Action has been started on regulations which will permit the entry of Canadian cattle, sheep, other domestic ruminants, and swine, and fresh, chilled, or frozen beef, veal, mutton, lamb and pork. Restrictions applying to other animal products and hay also will be removed.
The United States border has been closed to such imports since February 25, 1952, when the Canadian government announced the appearance of foot-and-mouth disease in the province of Saskatchewan. Strong measures adopted by the Canadian officials, which included quarantines, inspection, slaughter of diseased and exposed herds, and disinfection of premises, confined the disease to a relatively small area of that province. In addition to the original infection near Regina, two subsequent appearances of the disease nearer the United States border were brought under control without spread to other premises. The last infection was found on April 28 and the infected animals were slaughtered three days later.
The same prohibitions and restrictions applying since February 25 will continue in effect until the new order becomes effective. This applies to susceptible game animals as well as domestic livestock.
This is the report as put out in Washington and we received it on Saturday last.

I should think the place to comment on that would be when the estimates of the Department of Transport are up for consideration. In so far as the other matter is concerned, conditions at Port aux Basques, which are said to be disgraceful: I visited Port aux Basques this summer and I did not find conditions too good, but I would remind my hon. friend and the house that there is a tremendous amount of construction going on there for new terminal facilities. The Canadian National Railways have been given the job of building the facilities. It is just to remedy the present position that they have been put in charge of the operations. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DESIGNATION "OFFICERS OF THE CROWN"
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to a question which was asked last Thursday, November 27, by the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall), in these terms:
I should like to know what members of the cabinet are considered officers of the crown. If there are any members of the cabinet who are not in that category, who are those specific ministers of the crown who are not so considered?
I have drafted an answer to that question after speaking to the hon. member and finding out from him that what he had in mind was a recent decision by the president of the exchequer court to the effect that the Secretary of State is not an officer of the crown within the meaning of that expression in paragraph (c) of section 30 of the Exchequer Court Act, which gives the court jurisdiction in all cases in which a demand is made or relief sought against any officer of the crown for anything done or omitted to be done in the performance of his duties as such officer. I have no reason to suppose that the court would not hold similarly in the case of any other cabinet minister, that he is not an officer of the crown within the meaning of that expression in section 30 of the Exchequer Court Act. This decision should be regarded as the law of Canada so long as it stands unreversed by a higher court, but it applies of course only to paragraph (c) of section 30 of the Exchequer Court Act.

Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) rose to take part in this debate on Thursday of last week, he prefaced his remarks by saying, as reported at page 134 of Hansard:
Today I propose to deal with boots, forks and rugs.

I could not help thinking that perhaps he was going to quote from "Alice in Wonderland":
Of shoes-and ships-and sealing wax-
Of cabbages-and kings-
Then somebody mentioned neckties-hundreds of thousands of them. In fact, there were so many neckties that if they were placed end to end they would stretch from the minister's office to the firehall in Winnipeg-a thousand miles of neckties.
The minister then went on to explain why it was necessary that large quantities of stores of clothing and equipment should be purchased.
Stores of clothing and equipment were required for mobilization purposes. Everybody, of course, knows that large quantities of stores are required for mobilization purposes, and it is the duty of the government to provide those stores. But it is also the duty of the government to buy those stores in the most economical way possible. In order to attempt to prove his case the minister placed a great many figures on the record. But one set of figures which he did not give were those which would indicate what articles have been sold at bargain prices in the last few years through such organizations as War Assets Corporation. From the return which was made to this house in the early part of 1949, we know that the government had received no less a sum than $454 million for goods that it had sold at bargain prices. Or course in those days the word "stockpiling" did not enter into the minister's vocabulary.
Today I am not going to pursue that subject any further. I want to speak about another matter which affects the reputation of an officer and this country's standing in the sphere of international affairs and co-operation, in that it is in respect of the question of national defence. When the public is aroused by some particular incident and the government of the day gives only vague replies, a certain responsibility rests upon Her Majesty's opposition. When the public conscience feels uneasy over the treatment of one of its public servants, then it is again the duty of the opposition to ask for further clarification on that point. I intend this afternoon to ask for further clarification in the case of a brilliant young officer whose career was cut short suddenly in the middle of last summer. I refer to Brigadier A. B. Connelly, who was recalled from Korea and was retired at the age of 44.
Suspicion has been aroused because the government endeavoured to hide the fact that he was being recalled, and that he had been retired. It was only because of a news
The Address-Mr. Pearkes release in a foreign newspaper, the Chicago Tribune, that the facts-or at least some of the facts-regarding this case leaked out. The only definite information given by the Department of National Defence is in a release made by Mr. W. H. Dumsday, director of national defence public relations. He gave, I presume on instructions, the following release:
Brigadier Connelly is on retirement leave which will extend over a period of some months. The department does not normally give reason for retirements, except that senior officers are retired when there is no further suitable employment for them. With regard to the report that he was retired for his failure to immediately notify the Canadian government of the intention to use Canadian troops on Koje island, the department has no comment.
As appears in a dispatch in the Regina Leader-Post of October 7, 1952, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said that he could neither confirm nor deny the report that the Koje incident was involved in the retirement. Then the release states, in inverted commas, "I know nothing about it," he said. That is, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that he knew nothing about it.
However, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) of course does know all about this case, and he has made no statement over his own signature. There have been press comments and statements. The Victoria Daily Colonist refers to-
-a report from Ottawa published in a great many papers over the signature of Gerald Waring in which he says that the army has not even admitted officially that Connelly was sacked because he failed to advise the government last May that a company of Canadian soldiers was being sent to riot-torn Koje island to help guard prisoners of war.
Then it goes on to say:
However, high-ranking officers say that it was the "immediate cause" of Connelly's retirement.
I do suggest that by this silence and these rather cowardly insinuations the reputation of this officer may have been damaged, and his opportunity of finding employment, now that he has been forced to retire from the army, is handicapped. It is for these reasons I feel that the public of Canada and the members of the House of Commons are entitled to a full and clear statement.
It should be noted that Brigadier Connelly did not retire. He was retired, and retired eleven years prior to the time when, under normal circumstances, he would have reached the age limit for retirement. It is also to be noted that there have been other promotions made from lieutenant-colonel or colonel to the rank of brigadier, since the time of Brigadier Connelly's forced retirement.

So the public are asking why this has been done. Can they be assured-and they want to be assured-that their public servants, particularly those on active service overseas, are treated with absolute fairness? They are asking why this promising career has suddenly been cut off, after this officer had been educated at great public expense. He attended the Royal Military College at Kingston, an educational establishment maintained very largely by public funds. After having done exceptionally well in his four-year course at Royal Military College, he was given further education at public expense by being sent to McGill university. In 1931 he joined the permanent force and, in the course of his years of service, attended various other schools of instruction.
When war broke out in 1939 he went overseas and soon rose to the rank of senior engineer officer in the first Canadian division. He was then transferred to the position of senior engineer officer in the fourth armoured division and, shortly after that, promoted to the position of chief engineer of the first Canadian corps.
Then he was selected to command all the engineer reinforcements of all the Canadian forces in the United Kingdom. Then he became deputy chief of staff in London, and as such was responsible for the return of the Canadian troops remaining in the United Kingdom after the cessation of hostilities. In all I believe he spent some seven years out of this country on active service in Europe.
When he came back he was first of all made deputy adjutant general and then, because of his engineering experience, in 1948 he was selected to be the commander of the northwest highway system. As all hon. members know, the northwest highway system administers the Alaska highway which runs from northern British Columbia into the Yukon. Many glowing reports have been made to the house, particularly by the hon. member for Yukon-Mackenzie River (Mr. Simmons) and Cariboo (Mr. Murray), as well as by the ministers concerned, as to the importance of that great highway both from the point of view of national defence and from that of the economic life of the country.
I know that during Brigadier Connelly's tenure of command in the northwest highway system he was personally visited by members of this government. I never heard any complaint as to the work being done on that highway system; in fact, the contrary has been the case. In an address delivered in the

house by the hon. member for Yukon-Mackenzie River these words are used, as they are reported at page 1366 of Hansard for November 1, 1949:
The Canadian portion of the Alaska highway from Dawson Creek, British Columbia, to the Alaska-Yukon border, a distance of 1,223 miles, is maintained by the northwest highway system of the Canadian army and X wish, at this time, to commend them for the excellent job they are doing under the command of Brigadier Connelly, in keeping this highway open.
General A. G. L. McNaughton writes and says that he is personally familiar with Brigadier Connelly's work in connection with this section of the northwest highway system and says:
I consider that Brigadier Connelly is well qualified to assist in the organization and administration of important construction projects.
After two and a half years' service in the far north Brigadier Connelly was appointed commander of the Saskatchewan area where he remained until he was moved to a position of greater importance, namely, to be acting general officer commanding, prairie command. After the war broke out in Korea and the United Nations had established supreme headquarters in Tokyo, Brigadier Connelly was selected to be the liaison officer or military adviser from Canada to the United Nations supreme command.
I think hon. members will recognize at once that his has been a remarkable career, one which reflects great credit not only upon the officer concerned but upon the whole Canadian army. The public moneys which have been spent on his education would have been justified had he been permitted to complete his normal term of service.
The public want to know why he was retired on pension eleven years before the time at which he might ordinarily be expected to retire. He is still in good health, being a young man of only forty-four years of age; yet he is retired on a pension of more than $4,000 per year. Over the next eleven years that will amount to close to $50,000 of public money.

He is being retired on a pension of $4,400 a year and he still had eleven years to go. That would come close to $50,000 for that period. For the next eleven years we will get no value from his services. That is

why there is widespread feeling that Brigadier Connelly has been made the scapegoat for the Koje incident.
Let us examine Brigadier Connelly's position. He was liaison officer to the United Nations supreme headquarters situated at Tokyo where for the last year General Mark Clark has been in supreme command. The liaison officers serve under the assistant chief of staff of the eighth army who is particularly detailed to look after intelligence. General R. F. Ennis was the officer in charge of the United Nations Far Eastern command at that time so far as intelligence was concerned.
The duty of the liaison officer was to keen the government of Canada informed from such information as he could obtain with regard to contemplated operations and the progress of such operations. I presume he would write to the commanders in the field and would send in written reports or if necessary communicate with Canada by cable. I would emphasize that the liaison officer is not a commander.
I understand that this matter of sending troops to Koje was discussed with Brigadier Connelly and the commonwealth liaison officers in Tokyo and that before giving a definite answer, although it was hardly his place to do so, Brigadier Connelly suggested that the matter be referred to the commander of the 25th brigade, the officer designated as the senior Canadian officer in the Far East. The inference can be drawn from the press reports that this move was made while the matter was still in the consultative stage. Another inference which may be drawn is that Brigadier Connelly did report in his regular weekly reports to Ottawa that the matter of sending Canadian troops to share in guard duties at the prisoner of war camp on Koje island had been discussed with him and he had referred the matter to the commander of the troops.
Subsequently orders were issued through the regular channel of command passing down from the eighth army, from the commonwealth division to the commander of the Canadian brigade, that a company of troops would be required in order to give a more United Nations aspect to the guarding of the prisoners of war in that camp. It is fairly obvious that the troops did not consider this incident to be unusual. Canadian troops were under the command of the commonwealth division which in turn was under the command of the eighth army. Other detachments had been made along the lines of communication and certain Canadian troops were retained in Japan.
The Address-Mr. Pearkes
When the commander received the order he notified Ottawa in the ordinary course of events that he was sending one company of one of his battalions to assist in this guard duty. This house was informed on May 26 by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) of this fact, and I quote from page 2552 of Hansard of that day as follows:
On the afternoon of Thursday, May 22, the chief of the general staff received a telegram from the officer commanding 25th Canadian infantry brigade, Korea, to the effect that he had received an order from the first (commonwealth) division issued in accordance with a request from the United Nations command to post a company from the brigade to guard duty at the prisoner-of-war camp on Koje island, and that he was accordingly assigning a company from the Royal Canadian Regiment for this duty.
All of this had been in accordance with the plan for Canadian co-operation in the United Nations effort. We were part of the one effort striving for a common end. General Clark certainly had it within his authority to call upon any commonwealth troops to carry out any special duty within the area of the command that he considered was a reasonable task to assign to them. He was anxious to give a more United Nations aspect to this guarding of the prisoners of war. They were prisoners of war who had been captured by United States and commonwealth troops. In fact many of them had actually been captured by the Canadian forces. The continuation of the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs reads as follows:
The Canadian government therefore views with concern the dispatch of a company of the 25th infantry brigade to Koje island without prior consultation with the Canadian government . . .
Apparently the government seemed to go off rather half-cocked at that time because they issued this protest to Washington without taking time to discover whether the matter of sending a company to the Koje prisoner-of-war camp had been discussed with the commanders in the field or with the liaison officer. Faces were rather red when Washington came back and said that this matter had been discussed, that they had discussed it in Tokyo, and that the commander of the 25th brigade had been informed and had raised no objection.
It would appear that the government was embarrassed by this incident and they did not hesitate to let it be known that they had been embarrassed. So a whipping boy had to be found. Of course the darling of the government could not be chastised. Somebody had to take the beating for him. It may have been an error in judgment on the part of Brigadier Connelly when he did not send back by wire the fact that the matter

The Address-Mr. Pearkes of sending a company of Canadian troops to Koje island was being considered and merely reported it in a written statement, but it would hardly seem that one such error in judgment would be full and sufficient justification for cutting short the career of an officer who had already rendered such distinguished service and from whom the people of Canada might well expect to have additional valuable service rendered.
The opinion held by the United Nations officers under whom Brigadier Connelly was serving in Tokyo is of the very highest. I have a copy of a letter signed by General Mark W. Clark, the general in supreme command there. It is dated August 25, 1952, is addressed to Brigadier Connelly, and reads as follows:
Upon your departure from this command I wish to express to you my appreciation for the outstanding service you have rendered to the United Nations cause during the past ten months. Your unfailing courtesy, co-operative attitude and efficient handling of the tasks pertaining to your assignment have been of material assistance to this headquarters.
Then Brigadier Connelly's immediate superior, Major General Ennis, took the trouble to write directly to the Minister of National Defence expressing his deepest regret at hearing of Brigadier Connelly's pending departure.

In this letter, dated August 6, 1952, General Ennis says:
Never have I had the opportunity of working with a representative of an allied country that has given me more satisfaction and pleasure. Brigadier Connelly's impeccable honesty, diplomacy, sincerity, courtesy, humility and devotion to his country have won for Canada and for himself the highest respect from all United Nations representatives in this command.
He goes on to say:
We, your neighbours to the south, feel a great sense of pride and assurance in the future when we have the privilege of associating with such outstanding soldiers of the Canadian army.
He concludes by saying:
Those of us who have been closely associated with Brigadier Connelly during this past year wish him continued success in what will unquestionably be an outstanding military career.
That outstanding military career has suddenly been cut short. I repeat that in my opinion Brigadier Connelly has been used to cover up government embarrassment. He has


been retired from the service without justification, his character besmirched by innuendoes. I think this is a particularly vicious example of the government policy of concentrating control in Ottawa. To my knowledge it has already had a bad effect upon the morale of the troops. Commanders feel that their initiative is restricted, that they must refer every little detail to Ottawa thousands of miles away. Surely the question must be answered: Are we in or are we out of the United Nations Organization?
I cannot help thinking that, if the government had been honest with itself, then instead of retiring Brigadier Connelly the real blunderer would have been promoted to the other place. All I am asking is that the government make amends for the wrong it has done to this promising officer. Let right be done now. Let further employment be found for him so that the people of Canada may still have the benefit of the money they have spent on his education and the experience he has gained in the service of his country.
I want to touch briefly upon one other matter having to do with the question of national defence. Last August a new instruction was issued entitled "Regular Officer Training Plan". It laid down the means by which assistance would be given to selected students to obtain academic standards suitable for a career in the regular army. The instruction reads in part as follows:
This entails a guarantee of a minimum of two years university training beyond senior matriculation or equivalent to selected students who are enrolled as members of the active force and who remain in good standing from both academic and military viewpoints.
It goes on to say:
In addition to a special scale of pay, the assistance to students will consist of payment of tuition and all essential fees, books and instruments, required during the periods spent at academic training.
It explains that this training may be carried out at such military training establishments as the interservice colleges, R.M.C., Royal Roads and the college at St. Johns, Quebec. It lays down the scale of pay that they will receive while taking such training. During the first year they will receive $30 a month and the second year while they are serving in camps $170 a month. The point I want to make is referred to particularly in the next paragraph, which deals with the Defence Services Pension Act, and there it is stated that, as members of the forces, all officer cadets are eligible for the benefits prescribed in the act. Service from the date of enrolment, including time spent at university and at summer training, is pensionable service.

I have no quarrel with the conditions as laid down. I recognize that every effort is being made to obtain officers for the services and to give them a thorough education; but an anomaly does exist in that there will be officers still in the active army who passed through those colleges last year and in years previous who will not be able to count their service at service colleges towards pension. The young man taking advantage of this scheme, as promulgated on the tenth of August of this year, will have a very decided advantage over his fellow officers who are serving in the same units at the present time. Therefore, I would ask the minister if an amendment could not be introduced into the necessary acts in order to allow service at the interservice colleges to be deemed to be service in the forces-so that members who are now in the active force may have the same advantage as these new officers who are going in. Officers who are now serving in the active army will then also be allowed to count as pensionable service periods they spent at Royal Military College and elsewhere.
I think it is a reasonable request. In many respects service at the colleges is regarded as military service. The cadets are subject to military discipline, Queen's regulations, and so forth. They swear allegiance to the crown and if they receive injury through accident while they are at the college they receive a pension in much the same way as any soldier who suffers injury through accident. I think it would be only fair to those officers who have passed through these colleges and who, in many respects, do not get the same advantages as will be given the younger men who will be going through from now on. Those serving in the active army today should be granted the right to count their service at the colleges as pensionable service in exactly the same way as those who are now and who will be in the future passing through the colleges.

By coincidence I follow a distinguished and gallant army officer. I am a good friend of his and also of the gentleman referred to as being formerly in charge of the Alaska highway and northwest service command. Therefore I am very hesitant as a layman to make any comments further than to say that in these days all sorts of things are being said about army officers. Over the week end I had the opportunity of reading a book, the work of a distinguished Canadian author, which purported to be a biographical sketch of a former prime minister of this country. I see the statement made in that book that at a certain time certain army officers were in
The Address-Mr. G. M. Murray revolt against the crown, against the government and against the prime minister, and that there was a mutiny in the Canadian army. That is stated in so many words.
I was shocked and surprised to find that such a statement should have been made and that no one has risen to contradict it. I must refer to the book here, and I am probably doing good work for the publisher in referring to "The Incredible Canadian", which goes on and refers to all kinds of people here and pays "compliments" to the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. It is surprising to those of us who were his humble followers over the period of his public life to read such things. Statements in the Chicago Tribune and books of this kind should be carefully studied before they are accepted as truth.
Mr. King is referred to on one page of this book as the "lord high executioner" in relation to the position with regard to Colonel Ralston at a very important period during the war. The inference is that Colonel Ralston was ruthlessly slaughtered and set aside by that cruel and relentless man, Mackenzie King. I am not willing to accept that statement simply because I see it in print here. In another place in the book Mr. King is referred to as a grasping, mean little man; at another, as Mr. Uriah Heep, the most despicable character in all the works of Dickens. You will remember that Mr. Heep was "an 'umble man"-"always at your service, sir". At another point Mr. King is referred to as an old spinster and at another point he is referred to as man with a mailed fist sending people to slaughter; a liar. Well, that is a word that is seldom heard in parliament although it is often heard out on the hustings. He is referred to as a conniver, a schemer, a ruthless-I would almost say "monster" from reading the book -a lover of luxury, a gourmet, and a spiritualist.
It would be unfortunate in the affairs of this parliament if anything like that were to be allowed to go unanswered-although who am I to answer it? A student of Liberalism for many years as I have been, and a follower of Mr. King throughout, and a close observer too-I admit I am thirty years too late getting into the House of Commons but that is another story-I regard him as having been a great humanitarian, a stout champion of the poor, and while he was branded as a pacifist by some of his enemies, of course, I will say he was a Christian gentleman. He was a diplomat and he may have been a negotiator, but he was a very unselfish, very modest man, simple in his habits, a man who lived in a very modest way. Anyone who goes

The Address-Mr. G. M. Murray out to Kingsmcre and looks over the little cottage in which he died will see that. They will see the rugged stony acres where he had his walks. About the only enjoyment the man must have had was taking walks over the hills back of Kingsmere and watching the sunset. It is regrettable that such things are said of this outstanding man, outstanding in the affairs of this country, of the United Nations and of the world.
This afternoon when we were paying tribute to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) I wondered whether he was dead, from the fine things that were being said in the house. I want to tell some of these leaders over here that it is another grim feature of death when, three years after a prime minister of this country is placed in his coffin, circulation is given to literature which tends to belittle him in the eyes of the public. It is a very sad commentary upon our country. I hope that the time is not far distant when certain volumes will be published which are based upon the facts as contained in Hansard or other official records concerning that man's life, so that that will be the story that will go into the libraries of the land and not a book, as I say, that is calculated to break down and destroy the reputation of a great leader of this country.

The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard says that by their works ye shall know them. I think a further applicable reference would be that you do not gather figs from thistles. The great contributions of this statesman to our country are evidence of the man he was, and the position he will undoubtedly hold in history.
Turning to military matters, I had in mind making some reference to the Alaska highway, which is part of the northwest highway system. Anything that the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) said about the officer responsible for the management of the Alaska highway was, I am sure, well said. The same could be said about Brigadier Geoffrey Walsh, who preceded him. These men, and the Canadian army, have done an excellent job in maintaining that highway. I hope that we shall follow the example of the United States with respect to the Alaska highway, and see that a hard surface is laid as soon as it is convenient to lay one. Hundreds of miles within the territory of Alaska have been paved, and I think it should be our policy to start at mile zero, lay down fifty miles of pavement, and continue that paving program throughout the length of the highway.

This highway was one of those war services which have been of tremendous value in the industrial and peacetime life of the country. We have heard of the oil development up in the Peace river territory in British Columbia, as well as the development of the vast natural gas resources. Access to these drilling sites has been made possible by the Alaska highway and that very costly bridge over the Peace river. In fact, I do not know how much of the oil and natural gas development is due to the discoveries made by the men who built the highway. The first gas well was discovered by a firm of road builders who drilled a well for water at their camp and were surprised when natural gas gushed forth. For a long time there was a huge torch burning in front of that camp, just as if nature were crying out and trying to advertise the natural resources that were there.
When test drilling was undertaken for the bridge, they contacted a certain series of rocks containing fossils which gave geologists information in drilling for oil. The first oil well was drilled a few miles from this bridge. It was an achievement which, costly as it was, is now opening up the country to agriculture, mining and the peacetime development of the country.
There is a recent development to which I should like to refer, and that is the loss of so many aircraft between the United States boundary and the territory of Alaska. This leads me to say that there is a genuine need for a railway running north from Prince George in the direction of Alaska. The position now is that the United States is endeavouring to establish an airlift from Montana and the army camps to the south of the international border to the territory of Alaska. Such an airlift would cover a distance of between 1,500 and 2,500 miles, and in bad weather it is questionable whether such an airlift could be maintained. It is well to experiment with it. It is well to try to discover whether certain things could be done.
The loss the other day of an aircraft with fifty-two persons aboard, after flying across British Columbia, was a very regrettable thing. Some days before an aircraft with thirty-nine persons aboard went down, and a great number of lives have been lost on what I think is the foolhardy policy of the United States government in attempting to sustain an airlift from the United States to the Alaska border. I believe that General Eisenhower will probably have something to say about this matter, because there are few men who are better acquainted with that territory than that distinguished army officer.

On repeated occasions he visited the highway as well as the airports, and undoubtedly if we are to have security in the northwest the present airfields and highway will have to be supplemented by a modern railway running from Prince George. Such a railway, like so many of the things that have been carried out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) as a wartime measure, would turn out to be a great peacetime achievement, because it would open up the extensive valleys to great mining industries. You already have the oil along that route.
In the interval since we were here before I made a journey from Prince George in my riding a distance of 360 miles over the Parsnip and Finlay rivers to Fort Grahame and Fort Ware. This journey was made by boat, and I wish to say to you that we passed through magnificent country in which the agricultural possibilities are as good as they must have been in the Ottawa valley in the very early days of the settlement. In the whole 360 miles, we met about six white people and probably twenty Indians. Now, that is the Great Trench, as it is called by engineers. It runs due north and south from Prince George to Whitehorse. In that valley the United States army made a survey for a railway, and I believe such a railway should at some time be built through Sifton pass and north to Whitehorse and Alaska. Then, an armoured train carrying troops or civilian personnel could roll right from Puget sound through Vancouver to Prince George, Whitehorse and on to Alaska. I do not know why there has been a cooling off towards the idea of building that railway, but I am sure that in due course it must be built if we are to make this place secure and give the maximum amount of protection north of Edmonton.
I do not want to understate the fine defensive organization which is up there now. The airports are being well maintained and communication systems are being established. They are most modern in character. I have it on the authority of some very qualified army men that if an army of 150,000 men were to be placed in Alaska for the defence of that part of the continent, they could not be supplied by a highway or by airway and a railway would be an absolute necessity in order to provide supplies, munitions, guns and so forth for the service of such an army.
The riding which I have the duty to represent was given a high honour, during the early fall, when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself came through and paid us a visit. He travelled by air and came into Prince George from Prince Rupert. While he was there for only three hours or a little
The Address-Mr. G. M. Murray bit more, he endeared himself to a great many people. We had a fine audience out to greet him. There were probably 5,000 people there. Some wise strategists said that there should not be any political speeches, so that restriction cut me out of the program fairly well. All I could do was to go with the chairman of the board of trade and his worship the mayor, to see that the Prime Minister was given a good luncheon and that he was enabled to meet the people.
At the great public ground there the little children gathered around with their parents; there were many thousands of them. It was a perfect day. The Prime Minister proceeded to make his address. He said that he was not going to make any political references because it was sort of understood that this was more or less a personal visit. He went on and talked about Canada, our need of being good Canadians, and so on. Many of his listeners were children, of course. He said, "You know, down at Ottawa we try to conduct the government of the country in such a way as to safeguard your interests and to pass along to you young children who are here a better country than that which we received when we came into power". Just then, a dog came up in front of the platform, barked three or four times and then began to growl. The Prime Minister paused and then he said, "Don't you growl, because if our kind of good government is carried on, the bone which you get will have a lot more meat on it than was usual before we came into power." That is just a little human interest incident that shows the wit of the man and the gift which he has in greeting people of all ages and all conditions and moving among them.
After his speech he went out among the audience. I suppose he met probably 500 of those children in the concourse before him. How he does it, I do not know, but he has a smile for this one, shakes hands with that one and moves among the people. There is no necessity for any police to be around for his protection. We got him back on his plane in good time. He remarked upon the magnitude of the country over which he had flown from Prince Rupert, over that Alcan dam and up along towards Grande Prairie and Edmonton, a vast country where there is limited settlement. If I have any criticism at all to offer of the government benches it is that during the interval we have been here we have not paid enough attention to putting settlers-and by that I mean people who are fit to take over land-on that land or in that part of the country.
I know there are headaches and all that sort of thing in getting newcomers in here

The Address-Mr. G. M. Murray from Europe, from the United States and elsewhere; but we should have embarked upon a plan of settlement. I hope that in the next parliament that will be done. There are vast areas in there awaiting settlement. The resources are already well proved. In the Peace river block in British Columbia alone we will turn out, I suppose, eight million bushels of grain this year. You will remember that 20 years ago Sir Henry Thornton said that if we got ten million bushels in the entire Peace river country he would build us a railway. I hesitate to ask Mr. Donald Gordon to build a railway in there, but if there are that eight million bushels in the Peace river block, I will bet that there are 58 million in the entire Peace river country which would be served by a railway from there down to the Pacific coast. The present back-haul to Edmonton is expensive. It is retarding development.
As I say, we need settlers there. I think that we should draw the line at bringing any more foreigners into Canada and putting them in the cities. They have come and have brought along with them their skills, their knowledge of the various trades and so on, and some of them have been extremely valuable acquisitions. But if we want to do them and ourselves a service, we should fill up some of these vacant valleys that I have mentioned up in my riding and in those other ridings on the northern frontier of this country. We should have more people from the province of Quebec up in there, because the farmers from Quebec-who are trained and are familiar with the handling of livestock, grain and so on, who know how to use a broad-axe and can file a saw-could go in there with little capital and, with the roads that are now built and the facilities, that are now there, could establish new communities.
I repeat what I have said before, namely that I think such settlement would support the military effort. I am not one of those who are greatly enthused over the Korean situation. We are there and we have got to stay there; we have a job to do. It is a vast problem out there on the Pacific. Unless miracles are performed, we are going to be in there for a good many years to come. What is more sane, then, than to settle these valleys in the northwest, in those regions which are close to the Pacific? Get a population in there and allow them to prosper under a good sane government, have a few federal buildings built now and again when the hon. member for Cariboo asks for them, give them the other facilities which are necessary for carrying on the affairs of the country, and we will make a great contribution to Canada and to our allies.

I am aware of the fact that this is probably the last session of this parliament. I find that the time has passed rapidly. It is later than we think. I do not know what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and his associate will bring back from the commonwealth conference in England, but a good many of our people up in the northwest would like to see an early election. They point to the fact that the coronation is to take place in June. The government has outlined its program fairly well. Its policies are fairly well understood. The advice that I receive from my friends there is not to be overholding tenants but to urge the ministers to go to the country as early as possible so as to get another mandate to carry on good government in Canada. Some of them also said that in 1897, when Queen Victoria enjoyed her great jubilee, Canada sent over to England a distinguished prime minister to take part in those festivities, in the person of the then Mr. Wilfrid Laurier. With all the other leaders from the colonies or from the empire, he was there in attendance at those festivities. The record from that time up till now is of Canada steadily progressing as a member of the British commonwealth and as a great and prosperous land. My friends are saying that we should have an election and, if possible, send Mr. St. Laurent over to London so that he could follow in the footsteps of Laurier and represent this country at the crowning of the young sovereign. That would be my message. I hope that, before the summer is over, the election will be held and that the opinion of Canada will be taken on those great issues which have been so properly put before parliament since 1949.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak in support of the C.C.F. amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne and to speak more particularly upon the health insurance plan which the members of my party have put forward at this time, especially one phase of it. The care of the sick and the helpless is surely something with which we should be concerned. Indeed, I suppose it is the yardstick by which one can measure to what extent we are humanitarians or, perhaps, practical Christians. The survival of the fittest may be a perfectly good animal law, but we think that the care of the ill should surely be a human obligation.
Then, too, the benefits of healing must not be the sole prerogative of the privileged, as at least to some extent it is today. There are those who by reason of age, by reason of accident, by reason of a weak constitution or

by reason of the vicissitudes of illness must be cared for, and we cannot pass by on the other side.
In this connection I should like to divide the public into several classes. First we have the medical men, the scientists, the technologists, the nurses, those people whose services are at the disposal of the ill. At present, under our way of doing things, there are too few of these; and the fact that they are scarce in number adds at least in some cases to the price of their services, a price which many people find to be at a level they cannot afford.
Then among the general public there are those who, by their extra ability, by reason of good health or just through plain luck are able to obtain and to pay for, without limit, such medical services as they need. Those are the fortunate few. But we come then to the great middle group, a group for whom the fear of illness is always like an overhanging shadow, the group who know that a serious operation or a protracted stay in a hospital means for them and their families not only illness and pain but also economic ruin.
As I said, the great masses of the people fall into that category. What they want, what they would like to have now, is some insurance against such unfortunate contingencies. When I first came in contact with this sort of thing I was homesteading in northern Saskatchewan among a group of people who had gone up into that rough country to try to hew out a life for themselves. They went there with an axe, a grub hoe and, if they were fortunate enough, a team of oxen and a walking plow.
I saw there what it means to have no medical attendance, to live 42 miles from a railway. I recall having sold the municipality three-quarters of an acre on the side of a coulee as an addition to the graveyard. I can remember on cold winter nights when there would be a knock on my door. My neighbour would be there, and we would go out to the graveyard with a stable lantern and dig another grave on the side of that little hill, perhaps to bury the mother of a family. Perhaps that family had decided to take a chance, because they knew if they went for a doctor and brought him that considerable distance, and learned that it was a case for hospitalization, they would be crippled in their attempt to get on their economic feet, if I may so describe it, and would be set back for years and years. So they took the chance, and as a result they buried another Canadian mother, and perhaps an unborn child. We were very anxious about immigration in those days; we encouraged it. But we buried
The Address-Mr. Knight a great many Canadian babies and their dead mothers, when we should not have had to do it.
The third group I have in mind are the poor, the indigent, the maimed, the halt and the blind, those who are unable to take care of themselves, the victims of untoward circumstances, the victims of their own disabilities, or, if you like, sometimes of their own inabilities. They, too, are human beings; and no nation which vaunts its Christian philosophy can afford to neglect them, particularly in a Canada so blessed in its natural resources and its wealth. We cannot pass them by on the other side.
In the old days there was the charity ward, the infirmary, the poorhouse. I believe the people of this land are individually entitled to health services, in so far as they and their neighbours, speaking nationally, can afford to provide them. I believe my interest in education has been well established in the house; but let me say that while I consider education important, I consider of even greater importance the health of the people. I believe each Canadian is as much entitled to health, in so far as it can be provided, as each Canadian child is entitled to a free and full education.
All hon. members are old enough to have witnessed something of the ravages of disease, and the physical and economic ruin which in most cases are its results. It is enemy number one in the life of the nation, and the entire resources of the nation must be massed in battle against it. Science and the medical profession are embattled against it now, but I suggest embattled against it under handicaps.
I wish to pay tribute to the medical profession. My own father was a doctor, and perhaps I would have been one, too, had I not been in a preferred position to witness, and to come to dread, the spectacle of human misery brought about by suffering. Among my earliest recollections is the clanging of the night bell in the quiet and dark of the night and then, a few minutes later, the clop-clop of the sharp-shod mare on the stones of the street, taking my father out upon his errand of mercy, perhaps in the rain or the snow, and in an open vehicle.
I pay my tribute to him here, and to those other noble-souled doctors like him. He did more work for nothing than work he was paid for. Occasionally when he found it difficult to meet his own financial obligations he might say to us, in the morning at the breakfast table, "You know, I really ought to send some bills to those people"-but I do not think he ever did.
1 do not believe the doctors of today make such sacrifices; and let me hasten to add that
218	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Knight I do not think they should have to. In any event, free services to some mean eventually the higher cost of services to others. I think a doctor should he paid for all his work, and that fee should come out of the collective purse of the nation, where the amount of payment would be based upon the ability to pay.
We have not enough medical services; we have not enough doctors. Sometimes it is as difficult to see a doctor today as it would be to see the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I remember last June sitting in the office of an eye, ear and throat specialist in Saskatoon. While I sat there a farmer came in, walked up to the desk past twenty or thirty people who were waiting there, and said, "I want to see the doctor." The young lady in charge looked at him in amazement. "Have you an appointment?" No, he had not an appointment. He had never been in before but had come 200 miles. He said he would like to see the doctor. She told him that the best they could do was to give him an appointment on August 24, two months later. The argument that doctors are scarce is no argument against the immediate inauguration of a health plan. I shall develop this point later on.
There is one item I should like to deal with at once. Some people contend that the development of such a plan would somehow or other entail the loss of freedom. The only loss of freedom which would result would be in the payment of taxes to support such a plan. Of course those taxes would be compulsory, but the same can be said of any other form of taxation to which we are subjected. If there is any loss of freedom involved in the hospitalization fee in Saskatchewan, for example, apparently the people of that province are happy indeed about it. Last June they indicated that they were prepared to accept that loss.
There is not much freedom in the charity ward. Instead of any loss of freedom, on the contrary there has been in that province the opening up of new paths of freedom. There has been freedom from care and anxiety, there has been created that mental freedom which comes from security. This has been present since the passage of our hospitalization act. This feeling of satisfaction is so widespread in the province that it is only rarely that someone will get up, generally someone who is motivated by political intent, at a meeting and say, "I am strong and well, why should I pay $10 a year to provide hospitalization for someone else?"
On various occasions I have replied to people of that sort by saying, "I hope you will always remain strong and well. I am reasonably healthy and reasonably strong, but I


say to you that I shall be glad if I am able to pay $10 a year for the rest of my life even though I may not be ill a single day. I will consider that as not just insurance for myself for the rest of my life; I will be proud and happy to pay that for the benefit of some sufferer who may be less fortunate." I think that is the motive behind a medical health plan. There is still the question: Am I my brother's keeper? You can answer that just as you like.
Many of my colleagues have spoken on this plan during the present debate but there is one phase I should like to deal with, namely the shortages we have heard so much about. I shall have time to cover only the rather important one of hospital beds. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said that these shortages are likely to preclude any immediate inauguration of a national health insurance plan.
The Liberal party has behind it a long string of promises in regard to a national health insurance plan which have not as yet been implemented. I need not remind you that the first of those promises goes back to 1919. I should like to read a few quotations from Hansard of that and other days. A health insurance plan was promised in the speech from the throne in January, 1943 and also in the election of 1945. I should like to quote what Mr. Mackenzie Kang stated on May 14, 1948, as reported on page 3932 of Hansard. He said:
We have accordingly pledged ourselves to support a measure lor federal assistance in a nation-wide system of health insurance, to include assistance to the provinces lor preventive medicine.
That is fair enough. I could quote again from the same page where Mr. King is reported as saying that this measure represented the first stage in the development of a comprehensive health insurance plan for all Canada. Those grants were to pave the way for health insurance. They were to permit the necessary planning to be done. They were to eliminate the shortages which the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) now brings forth as the reason these promises cannot be implemented, particularly the shortage of hospitals, hospital beds and certain key personnel.
At that time Mr. King went on to say that the purpose of these grants was to assist the provinces in planning the extension of hospital accommodation and the proper organization of hospital and medical care insurance. Referring to professional training Mr. King said, as reported on page 3934:
The purpose of this grant will be to assist in making available the public health personnel which will be required in the development of an enlarged public health program in all fields. The grant will

also be available to assist in developing and training the personnel required for the operation of constantly expanding hospital services.
In discussing hospital construction, Mr. King went on to say:
Before health insurance can be established on an adequate basis, another development is essential. At the present time there is a tremendous shortage of hospital beds in Canada.
He then went on to say that the government would seek an appropriation for outright grants toward the construction of additional hospital accommodation. So much for Mr. King. It was made quite clear at the time he spoke and at the time the government program was announced in 1948 that the health grants were intended or designed specifically to pave the way for a nation-wide system of health insurance by eliminating shortages through inducing the provinces to undertake the required planning.
Four and a half years have gone by since 1948. Four and a half years of the program have been completed and what is the result? Apparently the government has no intention at the moment of introducing a health insurance plan and is still using the excuse of shortages in various fields as a reason why health insurance cannot be undertaken. The Prime Minister was reported in the Globe and Mail of September 6 last as having said in Victoria on September 5:
There isn't sufficient hospital space in Canada at present to make a federal health insurance program feasible ... I don't feel that the government has the right to give Canadians contractual rights to hospital treatment until there is sufficient accommodation in the hospitals to enable the government to fulfil the obligation. I don't feel that there is sufficient hospital space to enable all who have contractual rights to receive hospital treatment.
We in the C.C.F. party have long contended that shortages should never be allowed to delay the introduction of the scheme itself. In fact it is our contention that the graver those shortages are, the more urgent is the necessity of seeing that such services as are available are distributed according to medical need and not according to the ability to pay. When the government now says that there are not enough hospital beds to permit health insurance it is simply condemning itself, because this was a specific task which the government undertook when it gave these grants four and a half years ago. They undertook by giving these health grants to provide the hospitals, the hospital beds and the personnel necessary to permit the establishment of a health insurance scheme.
The C.C.F. is only too pleased to acknowledge the fine work that has been accomplished as a result of these plans, but as far as eliminating shortages of personnel
The Address-Mr. Knight and facilities is concerned the surface has not even been scratched. We claim that the most effective stimulus for the elimination of these shortages would be the introduction of a health scheme. The shortages will not be overcome until a vigorous attack is made on the problem as part of a nation-wide health plan. That has been the experience of every government that has undertaken comprehensive health measures. If the government waits until all shortages are overcome before introducing a health plan then we shall be waiting forever and no plan will be introduced.
I want to deal specifically with the most important of the shortages and the one which
1	think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) emphasized in his Victoria speech, namely the shortage of hospital beds. Reliable authorities-I may say I have documented what I am about to say and have the authorities here whether or not I quote them -have estimated that a minimum of 7-5 hospital beds per thousand of population is required. Indeed some authorities have estimated the figure to be somewhat higher. They go as high as 9 per thousand, including acute and chronic cases. But if we take the lower figure of 7 [DOT] 5 per thousand of population and calculate on the basis of our 1951 population, Canada should have a hospital bed capacity of 103,800 odd. We actually only have some 69,400, and I think that figure is too low, because it would necessarily imply certain duplication. It is a figure taken from the pamphlet "List of Hospitals" issued by the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Thus it is that on the basis of this standard -and, mark you, that is after approximately four years of the government's hospital building plan-there was still a shortage, according to their own figures, of 34,000 hospital beds in Canada. One of the things that must be remembered is that while there has been some increase in the actual number of beds there has been a corresponding or even greater increase proportionately in the population of Canada itself. In fact we have had an increase in population of roughly
2	million in the last five years, which years would be covered by these grants. This of course means an extra demand upon hosnital space. For example, between 1948 and 1950 the average daily patient population of hospitals increased from 48,000 to 53,000, an increase of 10 per cent. The reference there is to the annual reports of hospitals, 1948 to 1950, dominion bureau of statistics. The point was very well made in the annual report of hospitals for 1949 at page 10 in these words:
Although the number of reporting hospitals and their combined bed capacity has shown an increase

The Address-Mr. Knight in the past seventeen years, the ratio of bed capacity per 100,000 population for the same period has shown little variation.
Necessary though these grants were, we should ask ourselves what success they have had in bringing us closer to the ideal which prompted the giving of them. Of course there has been an increase in the number of hospitals built over the years, and no doubt we must give credit-and we give it cheerfully-to the hospital construction scheme of the government. But from 1948 when the grants were announced to 1951, four out of the five years, hospital bed capacity has only increased by roughly 13,500 beds, which is far short of the goal of 40,000 beds announced by Mr. King in May of 1948. This leaves approximately 26,500 beds to be completed in this last year of the program. I suggest to you, sir, that is a construction program for one year roughly twice the total of the past four years. It may be physically possible that that objective will be achieved but I would suggest it is highly unlikely.
