I took particular care to have all these figures documented. I have a complete list of such documentation which I will give my hon. friend when I have finished. I want to deal with another matter after I finish with this subject and I would rather not have my hon. friend give me a lecture at the moment. The fact of the matter is that the hospital grants program is going


to fall far short of its goal, and it is extremely doubtful if even half the five year goal will be reached.
Why is it that hospital construction is failing so badly? The only reason I can find is that the grants are too small. The program makes available $1,000 per bed for active treatment cases and $1,500 per bed for those cases which may be termed chronic or convalescent. But this is such a small proportion of the total amount required to build hospitals that it has not stimulated hospital construction sufficiently. In 1948-49, when the program got under way, hospital construction costs were approximately $10,000 per bed. That is a statement by an Ottawa man, Controller Paul Tardif, when speaking on March 14, 1949.
If we look at the composite index of wholesale building costs, including all construction materials and wages, we find that it has gone up from 200 in 1948 to 260 in mid-1952. If we use this as a measure of increase in hospital construction costs during that period, we find that construction costs would have gone up by at least $3,000 per bed in that period. In other words there would have been an increase over the period of $3,000 per bed, but the federal grant is only $1,000 per bed. At that rate it is no wonder that the program is failing in its objective.
Let me repeat that the only way to be sure that such shortages can be overcome is to undertake a nation-wide health scheme first. Far more generous grants would have to be made in connection with the program, and I want -to emphasize that the stimulus to increase construction arising from the increased demand for hospital services will do more than any other factor to ensure that the requisite hospitals are constructed quickly. This has been well demonstrated in my own province. When the C.C.F. government was elected in Saskatchewan in 1944 that province was short of hospital beds, as was the rest of Canada. It only had 3-75 hospital beds per thousand population. My authority here is the annual report of the Saskatchewan hospital service plan, 1951.

We have had some bold and imaginative action which, coupled with a lot

of hard work, resulted in a tremendous hospital construction boom. I shall say, too, for the benefit of my hon. friend who has interrupted me that a great part of that construction was undertaken before federal hospital construction grants were available at all. The result has been that hospital beds in Saskatchewan have increased from 3-75 per thousand in 1944 to 6-7 per thousand at the end of 1951. By the end of this year there will be well over 7 beds per thousand.
Saskatchewan, thanks to its inauguration of a provincial hospital scheme and a vigorous construction program undertaken in conjunction with that scheme, is the only province in Canada which has anything like adequate hospital facilities available. This experience, we think, should be applied in the federal field. The best stimulus, I repeat, that could be provided to overcome the hospital shortage would be the inauguration of a national health insurance program such as is advocated by this party.
A similar experience has been found in the United Kingdom in connection with their universal health services plan, the one they undertook in 1948. They too were faced with severe shortages of hospitals as well as personnel. But, in the three years after- note that I say "after" and not "before"-the inauguration of their program, they increased the number of staffed hospital beds by nearly 40,000.
In literally dozens of countries it has been the same story-insufficient doctors, hospitals, nurses, and so on. If they had waited until those shortages had disappeared they would be still waiting as we are still waiting in Canada, but they proceeded with their plans for health services. They introduced them themselves, and that introduction was the best stimulus to overcoming the shortages. It is the demand which creates the supply, and it is useless to build hospitals unless at the same time provision is made by which the general public can be enabled to pay for those services when they are provided.
I would like to have said a word or two about the shortage of nurses. Just as with hospitals, there have been shortages of facilities for training nurses. Other governments have found that the best method of dealing with those shortages is the inauguration of a health plan. In the United Kingdom the most acute shortage, as a matter of fact, was in the nursing field. In preparation for, and later as part of the national health service plan introduced in that country, working conditions were improved and pay was increased not only for nurses but also for other hospital workers. As a result of those measures and as a result of the better finan-
The Address-Mr. Knight cial circumstances of the hospitals resulting from the inauguration of the health plan- and by the way that is something we discovered in our province: the hospitals are no longer running behind financially-nursing staffs in the United Kingdom increased from 127,200 in 1947 to 153,100 in 1949. That is an increase of more than 20 per cent in a little more than two years. To my hon. friend I would recommend the reading of a new book by James Ross, "National Health Services in Great Britain, 1952".
In Saskatchewan the effort to increase the supply of nurses has been described in the Saskatchewan health survey report, volume 1, page 176, and I quote:
In 1945 a plan was instituted by the health services planning commission whereby the hospitals with nursing schools which could legitimately enrol more than their normal quota of nursing students would be paid a grant to defray the additional expense incurred in doing so . . . Since 1947 the costs of operating the schools of nursing have been recognized as hospital operating costs under the payment system of the Saskatchewan hospital services plan. As a result of these efforts there has been a substantial increase in enrolment in schools of nursing.
This is also a statement from the report:
From 1945 to 1949 there was an increase of 29 per cent in enrolment in schools of nursing in Saskatchewan. During the five years, 1945 to 1949, the increase in the number of students enrolled almost kept pace with the increase in the rated capacity of those hospitals.
With the improved conditions of nursing and with the active encouragement of the government in the manner indicated, the rate of withdrawal of nursing students in Saskatchewan has been reduced to 20 per cent, well below the rate in the rest of Canada, which is 33 per cent, and below the figure of 30 per cent for the United States.
The government says there are shortages and that it cannot undertake a national health insurance plan until the shortages are overcome. It is the C.C.F. contention that the government's program for overcoming these shortages will fail miserably, and that rather than a health insurance program being dependent upon the overcoming of shortages it will be the best single means, if not the only means, by which the shortages may be overcome. This applies not only in the two fields I have been discussing-hospitals and nurses-but also as far as physicians, dentists, psychiatrists, technicians and other personnel are concerned.
Sir, I have now to turn rather abruptly and hurriedly to another subject. I am almost compelled to raise it by the fact that I have a letter from the branch of the Canadian Legion in my own city, and I have

This afternoon I am going to follow a little different line of thought from the previous speakers. It has been most interesting during the past several sessions for me to watch the chief opposition party under the direction of its leader, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Drew), change direction many times in its attack on the Department of National Defence. In the fall of 1950, some months after the outbreak of hostilities in Korea, the Leader of the Opposition had this to say, and I quote from page 473 of Hansard for September 8, 1950:
Does any hon. member think that the men in the Kremlin are going to be greatly impressed by the news that some months from now we are going to have a special brigade available? In the face of their 175 fully mobilized divisions and their 350 divisions which could be in the field in a very short time, is one special brigade, with three or four thousand combatants, going to leave very much impression in their minds of the urgency, vigour and determination with which we are playing our collective part in the responsibility of saving freedom for ourselves and for others?
In actual fact the Department of National Defence extended its facilities so greatly that in the spring there was an announcement to this house of a $5 billion defence program.

This $5 billion was to be spent over a period of three years. In the fiscal year 1951-52 parliament authorized the Department of National Defence to spend $1,700 million. This was an extremely ambitious program, of which more than one-third was to be implemented in the first year. In spite of the fact that this program was extremely ambitious, the Canadian part of it was almost accomplished. The bulk of the $340 million odd which was not spent was made up of undelivered orders placed in the United States. It was later stated that all that Canada was behind in that defence program was the undelivered orders from the United States.
Then last spring, lo and behold, the Leader of the Opposition changed his tactics and played up the overtaxation theme, chiefly because of this surplus that had been built up. He refused to recognize that the bulk of that accumulated surplus was the underspent portion of the defence program. Some of the words that were used during that last session by members of the chief opposition party were "waste" and "inefficiency". Inefficiency was supposedly rampant in the armed forces and they spoke of large-scale looting, theft, fraud and incendiarism.
Then at the opening of this session and the beginning of this debate the Leader of the Opposition continued his charges of waste and inefficiency, and brought up* material that had been thoroughly covered in the defence expenditures committee last spring. He went further, and I quote from page 23 of Hansard for November 24, 1952:
This government has largely destroyed the effectiveness of the committee system established by this parliament for the examination of government expenditure by permitting and in fact encouraging the use of a majority of government supporters on those committees to deny any real opportunity to conduct effective inquiries.
It has been my privilege, Mr. Speaker, in the last two sessions of parliament to be a member of the defence expenditures committee. In the two final years, 1951 and 1952, $2 billion of the taxpayers' money was spent by the Department of National Defence. That is a great deal of money, and it came out of the pockets of our taxpayers, including the pockets of the taxpayers in my constituency. As a member of that committee I felt it was my responsibility to my constituents to assure myself as to whether or not that money had been spent to the best advantage.
Any other hon. members who are concerned would do well to read the third and final report of the defence expenditures committee of last session. I am going to quote one paragraph:
Mr. E. B. Armstrong, assistant deputy minister, Department of National Defence, gave a detailed
The Address-Mr. Weaver explanation of the control and accounting of materiel and stores in the Department of National Defence. In addition, the committee requested and obtained documents containing detailed information regarding thefts, frauds, fires and other write-offs in the navy, army and air force during the fiscal years 1950-51 and 1951-52. These documents contained a total of 182 pages of relevant information.
I hold in my hand those 182 pages of relevant information which were given to the committee on defence expenditures last spring. While the committee was sitting, certain figures were given. These figures which were given to the committee were commented upon later in the house by the Leader of the Opposition. I again quote from page 2329 of Hansard for May 19, 1952 where he said:
. . . but there have become available reports of theft, looting and fires, some of them incendiary, which have resulted in the last two years in a loss estimated by the Department of National Defence at a figure of more than $7 million.
He tried to leave the impression that this figure had resulted entirely from theft, looting and incendiary fires. Not only did he do that; he tried to leave the impression that this $7 million figure was greatly underestimated and should have been much greater, because a few lines further on he said:
If the accounting methods of the Department of National Defence report a loss of only $3,500 at Farnham, then the statement given of the total loss as in the statement prepared by the department, showing a loss of more than $7 million, should contain figures very much higher than it actually does.
I just wonder how much higher the Leader of the Opposition would have liked the people of Canada to believe they should have been, whether it was $5 million, $10 million or even perhaps $20 million.
Along with these documents I showed to the house there was a recapitulation giving the amount. The first heading was "Losses due to Theft or Fraud" and it gives the total sum for all three services at $85,809.75. The next item was "Losses due to fire", and the total for the three services was given at $5,205,970.54. Finally, the third item was "Other Write-Offs" amounting to $2,212,931.15. It is this figure for "Other WriteOffs" that I particularly want to deal with this afternoon.
I should point out that "Other Write-Offs" covers the units, the amount of the write-off, and the surplus taken on charge at the same time. There is also another column showing "Estimate of Total Holding" and a column showing the reasons for the write-offs. In these figures that I read out there was nothing to show how much had been taken on charge at the same time; and in the committee I asked that this figure be supplied. This

The Address-Mr. Weaver figure was supplied as $643,193.09. I will shortly give you the reasons I quoted it in this way.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) in the committee asked for a break-down of one of these items, and this break-down was filed in the committee as exhibit G. I will just mention two of these items. In stocktaking there was an item, three globe valves x 300 pounds. Those were written off. Right under that there is another item of three globe valves x 280 pounds, taken on charge. In other words, valves of the exact designation x 300 pounds were not there, but there were three valves with a slightly different designation and they were taken on charge. Another item was 12 globe valves 2" x 150 lbs. written off and another twelve valves with a slightly different designation taken on charge. The total written off in this particular exhibit was approximately $7,000 and the total taken on charge was approximately $6,600, so that there was a net write-off of just $452. This is carried all the way through the many documents-taking on charge an amount, as I gave you before, of $643,000 approximately, which naturally should have been subtracted from that figure. Then on going through ttrese documents it was found that among the things written off was one North Star aircraft valued at $225,000. This aircraft was destroyed by explosion. I will read from the remarks column where this information was given to the committee:
Explosion occurred while aircraft was being refuelled. It is believed that the N.C.O. who had removed the snow from the aircraft had accumulated electric static in his body and by kneeling on a broom and a piece of rag caused a spark which resulted in the explosion.
We are enjoying nice weather down here in Ottawa at the present time and we are all quite comfortable. I wonder whether those who have been so critical of the soldiers, airmen and naval personnel would remember that this aircraft was destroyed at Whitehorse in the Yukon.
Then there was damage in a crash, to a Lancaster aircraft, amounting to $78,000. Another item written off-I am not going to give the exact figures because it takes a great deal of time to do that; I will give round figures-was approximately $500 for the loss of propeller and anchor from a marine craft:
The propeller was lost while proceeding out Miramichi river. The craft returned to Chatham on the starboard engine. It was necessary to use anchors to hold the stem of the craft against the tide. One anchor had become caught in an old sunken crib and it was impossible to raise and recover the anchor.

I am sure hon. members will recognize that this item does not fall under any of the classifications of looting, theft or fraud.
Another item was $14,000 for radio equipment to be replaced following a fire in the Department of Transport control tower at Coral Harbour. I am sure that would not come under the heading of theft, fraud or looting. Here is another one that struck my fancy. This one amounts to approximately *$2,500 and is for the loss of 335 empty gasoline drums:
The loss occurred while being transferred to Norman Wells via Waterways. The loss is attributed to a storm on Great Slave lake.
That could bear no relationship to theft, fraud or looting. Then there was a figure of approximately $3,500 for other damage in aircraft crashes, including loss of wing tanks, parachutes, airmen's kits, and so on. Here is another one amounting to $16,000, gas written off in northern gas caches. These gas caches are spread over the Northwest Territories all across northern Canada. They are there and are used under circumstances of great urgency, usually when the thermometer is at a very low point. I am sure none of the airmen who get cold fingers trying to transfer gasoline from one of these caches far from civilization would like it thought that the figures of write-offs in these cases were included in the figures given to the committee on defence expenditures under the heading of thefts, frauds or looting.
Another item was for $10,000 of bridging equipment carried away by flood in British Columbia. There is a further item of $4,000 for bridging equipment damaged and sunk in British Columbia. Then there was a total of approximately $23,000 for accidental damage to vehicles and other equipment. Just to mention two of these items, there was one for $4,000 and one for $6,000 for aircraft engine damage.
Thus far I have overlooked one large item. In the figures given to the defence expenditures committee under this recapitulation there is included naval aircraft write-off for
1950-	1951 and naval aircraft write-off for
1951-	52. In one year it was $385,000 and in the other $670,000, or a total of $1,055,000. This certainly cannot be classed as theft, fraud, looting or incendiarism.
The figures I have given total $1,434,028.67. I have already explained the figure described as "taken on charge". That, added to the previous figure I have given, makes a total of $2,077,221.76. All these amounts must be subtracted from the figure given before, namely $2,200,000 odd. I have not begun to give all the things written off that are of a similar nature to the ones I have already

given. However, subtracting the total from the figure given for "other write-offs" we have left $135,709.39. It is only in this figure that there might be room for some dishonesty, along with some carelessness and perhaps some mistakes. But that is a far cry from $2,212,931.15.
Let us now consider the subject of fires. According to this recapitulation, losses due to fires in two years amounted to something more than $5,200,000. Among these were two large fires, one at Trenton with a loss of $2,300,000 and one at the 26th Canadian ordnance depot. These two losses totalled approximately $3,031,000.
These losses drew no special criticism from the committee. As a member of the committee I had all the information available, and I could see no reason to suppose that these were not in the same category as fires in other cities in Canada. In fact these fires were far below the rate of fires in six representative cities. This information was given to the house last session by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). But of all the fires listed in these documents there were one case of incendiarism and three cases of suspected arson, although they were not proven.
In this recapitulation I have allowed the three cases of suspected arson, in order to meet the conditions set out by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in the statement I read, where there was reference to theft, looting and fires, some of them incendiary. Meeting these conditions, the totals would now appear to be: losses due to theft or fraud $85,809.75; losses due to incendiary fires and suspected arson, $218,096.33, and other writeoffs where there might be room for some carelessness, dishonesty or mistakes, the sum of $135,709.39, making a total of $439,615.47.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a newly-elected member who was introduced to the House of Commons on the same day as was the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Deslieres) and the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider), I would indeed be remiss in my duty if I did not join hon. members on all sides of the house and extend my sincere congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne upon the able manner in which they have discharged their respective duties.
I crave the indulgence of the house if I find it necessary to confine myself to matters of purely local interest. I do so cognizant of the fact that there are those more able than myself who can discuss questions that are of major national or international importance. If I steer a somewhat homeward course it is done in the hope of better fulfilling the mandate which has been given to me by my constituents. I intend to speak about matters about which I know something rather than to trespass into unknown fields.
It is my intention to limit my modest contribution to this debate by dealing first with a passage from the speech from the throne which raises a matter of interest to the province of New Brunswick. I shall then centre the remainder of my remarks around certain policies and practices of the present administration which directly affect the primary industries of my own constituency of Gloucester.

The Address-Mr. Robichaud
In the speech from the throne it is indicated that parliament will be asked to make financial provision for a proposed new ferry service between Yarmouth, Nova Scotia and Bar Harbor, Maine. I preface my remarks at this point with the clear statement that my native province of New Brunswick has no animus against our neighbouring province of Nova Scotia. The fact is that the two provinces have many things in common. Ethnically our people spring from the same ancestry. Geographically we are neighbours and partners in the maritimes. Economically we have similar problems. New Brunswick, as you know, has always been ready to champion any cause put forth by our sister province which we felt would be conducive to the attainment of economic advantage. Let it be understood that the support of Nova Scotia in any maritime-wide effort has always been appreciated by every New Brunswicker.
However, when the announcement was made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) in November last that a contract for the construction of a vessel to operate between Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, and Bar Harbor, Maine, had been awarded to the Davie Shipbuilding Company of Lauzon, Quebec at a price of $3,926,000 we in New Brunswick were indeed deeply concerned. We realized that this project was the result of a most laudable effort by the Nova Scotia government to attract a greater number of United States tourists to that province by providing a short-route ferry between the points I have mentioned. Were the province of Nova Scotia to assume the greater part of the cost of the construction and operation of this ferry we in New Brunswick would have next to nothing to complain about, but as I understand the situation the provincial government of Nova Scotia has succeeded in convincing its counterpart, the federal government, that it should assume approximately two-thirds of the cost of construction as well as a substantial share of the cost of operating this ferry.
It is reported that the new ferry will have an over-all length of 345 feet 10 inches and a service speed of 18J knots. It will make one round trip a day during daylight hours and will have a capacity of some 600 passengers and about 150 automobiles. In announcing the award of the contract the Minister of Transport, according to a special press dispatch from Ottawa, was reported to have said that when in operation the new ship will add considerable impetus to the interchange of traffic between Nova Scotia and the New England states and will attract tourist traffic to the maritimes.


It would be most illogical to take issue with the first part of the minister's statement, as undoubtedly traffic between Nova Scotia and the New England states will be considerably increased by the proposed new service, but I am not prepared to concur in the second part of the minister's statement where he says that the car ferry will attract tourist traffic to the maritimes as a whole. The position we take in New Brunswick is that the proposed new service will prove detrimental to our tourist trade. The Moncton Times of September 26 put it tersely in an editorial as follows:
In committing the dominion government to such a bargain, Hon. Lionel Chevrier is directly discriminating against New Brunswick in its tourist industry. Or to put it another way, Ottawa is subsidizing Nova Scotia's vacation travel business to the detriment of a border province, and, therefore, is at once unfair and unjust to the latter. This federally-aided Bar Harbor-Yarmouth ferry will, unmistakably, funnel off from this province a very considerable volume of motor-visitor travel from U.S.A., and on which we have expended quite large sums of money to promote.
The people of our province, particularly those in the southern part, are gravely concerned over what they consider to be discrimination against New Brunswick on the part of the federal government. The general opinion is that the ferry short-cut will deprive New Brunswick of numerous tourist cars which otherwise would travel through the province en route to Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island. The New Brunswick tourist industry is bound to be affected by the new service, as a considerable number of United States tourists will take advantage of the ferry service and go to Nova Scotia rather than motor through the beautiful province of New Brunswick. Such being the situation as we in New Brunswick view it, are there any possible solutions in order to at least palliate our lot as a contributing partner to this project? It is suggested that the matter would be at least partly solved if arrangements could be made to operate the ferry on a triangular route including a call at the port of Saint John, New Brunswick, for instance. Again, if the former link between Saint John and Boston through the passenger liner service of Eastern Steamship Lines could be re-established, this, we submit, would increase the tourist traffic to the province of New Brunswick without too much interference from the proposed Yarmouth-Bar Harbor, Maine, ferry. However, as the matter now stands the province of New Brunswick is bound to lose in the deal.
We are unfairly called upon to contribute our share as a province of this dominion to a costly project which cannot but prove highly detrimental to our own interests. I

am fully aware of the principle that particular local interests or provincialism, if you want to call it that, must often be forgotten or sacrificed to bring about the attainment of a greater common good. Yet I cannot see any justification in a project involving a considerable expenditure of public moneys to which New Brunswick will have to contribute its share, whose resultant effects will necessarily prove detrimental to our province to the exclusive benefit of our sister province of Nova Scotia. I therefore feel that I am voicing the opinion of my province in protesting against this proposed large federal subsidy to the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor, Maine, ferry.
Coming now to the consideration of certain policies or practices of the government in so far as they directly affect Gloucester county, I must deplore the loss of markets for unmanufactured wood and underline certain policies or practices on the part of the Department of Public Works bordering on malfeasance and, most particularly, on nonfeasance, which are seriously hindering the expansion and development of our fisheries. The products of our forests have played a most important part in the economic development of our county. During the past few years one of the most profitable exports from Gloucester county, the Miramichi area, and from all our New Brunswick eastern ports down as far as Pugwash, Nova Scotia, has undoubtedly been our pit props.
Perhaps the main reason pit props have proven to be one of the most convenient resources on the farms of my own and other counties of the maritime provinces lies in the fact that almost every farmer has on his woodlot jackpine, spruce or fir, which are all adaptable to the making of pit props. One cord of pit props cut and peeled is a fair average day's work for our eastern farmers in their off-season spare time, and this represents the appreciable sum of $30. In 1948 total Canadian exports of pit props to Great Britain amounted to $7,580,399. In
1951	these same exports had fallen to $2,566,136. I dare say that most of these pit props, especially in 1951, came from the maritime provinces.
According to the latest available statistics the total value of pit props exported to the British market during the first nine months of
1952	has shrunk to $1,812,902. It may be said that competition from the Baltic countries and the scarcity of so-called "hard money" in Great Britain are responsible for this loss of markets. Nevertheless this is a situation which is bringing hardship to the people of my constituency and of other
The Address-Mr. Robichaud counties in the maritime provinces, and we naturally look to the federal government to do something about it.
There has also been a marked decrease in our exports of peeled and rough pulp-wood, as it is called, to the United Kingdom. Whereas our exports of peeled pulpwood to those overseas markets represented a dollar value of $1,846,297 in 1951, we only exported to the amount of $152,086 during the first nine months of 1952, or about one-twelfth of our 1951 export value. Similarly our exports of rough pulpwood fell from $1,383,607 in 1951 to a paltry $6,507 during the first nine months of the present year.
These figures, Mr. Speaker, are tragically eloquent in their significance to the pit-prop and pulpwood operators, to the woodsmen and the farmers of the northern and eastern parts of New Brunswick. Prospects for the coming year at the present time are on the dark and gloomy side. Britain's 1953 pit prop requirements will be mostly filled by Poland, Finland, Sweden and Russia. I am informed that we cannot expect any substantial contracts from Great Britain next year. This picture of our exports of unmanufactured wood is obviously far from rosy and promising for the coming cutting season. Already our newly elected government in New Brunswick, fully awake to the gravity of the situation, has taken active steps with a view to inducing the buyers in Great Britain to continue their patronage in pit props at least to the operators, woodsmen and farmers of New Brunswick. This problem is of such magnitude as to necessitate the direct intervention of the federal government and I therefore make a strong appeal to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to explore every avenue, every possible means of reopening the markets which we are losing in Britain to the great detriment of the woodsmen, farmers and operators of our maritime provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the recess I had been quoting statistics in support of the contention that we are faced with losing our British markets for pit props and pulpwood. In view of these considerations, which have had such an immediately unfavourable reflection on an important factor of the economy of my constituency, as well as that of many other counties in

The Address-Mr. Robichaud the maritime provinces, I certainly cannot endorse nor accept that part of the throne speech which states:
Our economic conditions remain favourable and the level of external trade is high.
I turn now to fisheries. In my maiden speech in this house I took a definite stand on behalf of the fishermen of the county of Gloucester. I stated then and I repeat now that fishing is positively one of our most important industries. For quite a few years the federal government has agreed to pay to the fishermen's loan board of the Atlantic coast provinces a subsidy of up to $165 per gross ton towards the construction of dragger or long-liner type vessels. In Gloucester county several draggers have been constructed under that arrangement. The subsidies provided by the federal government have certainly proved to be a good investment because landings and landed value of cod, and more particularly flatfish, have certainly increased since our fleet of draggers has been operating. Lately there has been a considerable increase in the landings of flounders particularly in the bay of Fundy and northern New Brunswick. With a ready market for these fish, the marked increase in the catch from 9,351,000 pounds in 1949 to 15,159,000 pounds in 1950 represented quite a substantial increase in revenue for our fishermen. In New Brunswick alone for the first nine months of 1952 the landed value of plaice and other flatfish was $174,000 as compared with $154,000 in 1951.
I think it is safe to say that most of those fish were caught by the Gloucester county dragger fleet in the course of their coddragging operations. In 1949, when the landings of cod and other ground fish showed a marked decrease, especially in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, our Gloucester county fleet draggers produced an increase of 2 million pounds over the preceding year. Those figures substantiate the contention that the new type draggers have certainly revolutionized the fishing industry in northern New Brunswick. There is an increasing demand for those draggers and it is my hope that the New Brunswick fishermen's loan board will continue to receive ever-increasing assistance from the federal government as this type of federal assistance has certainly proved to be a practical and efficient way of increasing the production of our deep-sea fisheries.
May I, at this stage, bring to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) a clause in the contracts heretofore entered into between the fishermen's loan board of


the province of New Brunswick and applicants for dragger type vessels. This clause has already given rise to numerous justifiable complaints on the part of dragger owners. I wish to refer to the contractual obligation under which our fishermen are bound to sell all their catch, if not to specified dealers then at least within the province of New Brunswick. This clause, in the dragger contracts, has always seemed to me most unfair to our fishermen. It borders, in my submission, on a clause in restraint of trade inasmuch as it gives local dealers an opportunity to agree on a set price which in some instances may be lower than market conditions warrant; and at the same time it forces our fishermen to sell at such a dealer's agreed or set price. I have been informed that draggers coming in from the fishing banks with a load could easily, in a few hours, cross the baie de Chaleur and sell their fish on the Gaspe shore at a price higher than the Caraquet or Shippigan dealers will allow them. Yet being bound by their contract they cannot avail themselves of such a profitable opportunity.
According to the September issue of the "'Monthly Review of Canadian Fisheries Statistics", the price received by fishermen for cod at Caraquet, New Brunswick, as at September, 1951, was 2J cents per pound as landed. During the same period cod commanded a price of 3 cents per pound at Souris, Prince Edward Island, 3 to 4J cents per pound at Halifax and 3J cents per pound at Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. As at September 15, 1952, our fishermen were receiving 3 cents per pound for cod at Caraquet when they could have sold the same cod at prices varying between 3J and 3f cents per pound at Souris which is a most accessible port for them, especially during the late summer and fall operations.
The above statistics clearly show a disparity of prices which is detrimental to our Gloucester county fishermen, bound as they are by the already mentioned restrictive clause in their contracts. The dragger fishermen cannot protest too loudly against this unfair situation, or when they can protest it is too late as they must sign their agreement before they can obtain a loan from the New Brunswick fishermen's loan board. On the face of it, however, this restrictive and mandatory clause in their contracts militates to the detriment of the fishermen and favours the dealers. I consider it my duty to bring this situation to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) with a view to obtaining his assistance and collaboration, so that our New Brunswick

The Address-Mr. Robichaud
fishermen's loan board may be induced to have this unfair clause deleted from all our dragger contracts.
I hope I have in no uncertain terms underlined the importance of the dragger type of vessel in the development of our deep-sea fisheries. This brings me to the problem of dragger operations and their effect on inshore fisheries, particularly along the coast of the baie de Chaleur. Numerous complaints have already been filed with the Department of Fisheries on behalf of several long-line fishermen in my county. According to the terms of condition 1 printed on the licence issued to draggers, no fishing operations can be carried on within one-half mile of boats or vessels fishing with hooks and lines or any stationary fishing apparatus, nor interfere with other methods of fishing. Unfortunately it is a well known fact that this regulation is disregarded by several small draggers, some of which come from the Quebec side of the baie de Chaleur during their fishing operations in our bay. Hundreds of dollars worth of actual damage to trawls and other fishing equipment have already been reported to departmental officials. Were we to add to these amounts the catch value of the fish lost as a result of the damaged gear and the time and labour involved in repair and replacement, we would realize that the fishermen who depend for a livelihood on inshore fishing along the coast of Gloucester county certainly have good grounds for complaint. We have been told that the problem is under active consideration. May I urge the Minister of Fisheries and his technical advisers to spare no effort in finding a solution to this important problem.
I am and always will be prepared to assist in promoting the best interests of our dragger fishermen. I am one of those who believe that these dragger type vessels are essential to the modern concept of deep-sea fish production. On the other hand I feel that I owe a duty to the no less deserving inshore fishermen who are entitled also to a full measure of protection and encouragement. Having approved the actual method of federally subsidizing the construction of dragger or small dragger type vessels, may I now suggest to the Department of Public Works some of the ways by which it can also assist in promoting and encouraging our fisheries in Gloucester county.
I have stated already in this house that the county of Gloucester has been sadly neglected by the present federal government, particularly with regard to certain public works which the people of my constituency consider essential to the full development of our fisheries potentialities. In the estimates
for 1952-53 there was an item of $32,000 for the dredging of Ferguson gully near Tra-cadie, New Brunswick. The dredging of this gully has been a perennial promise by Liberal candidates at every federal election since the turn of the century. The dredging of this gully is a matter of major importance to the fishermen of that locality. Although the moneys were voted at the last session, nothing has been done so far. How much longer shall the fishermen of Tracadie Beach and Big Tracadie river have to wait for the realization of this project?
Likewise, strong representations have been made to the Department of Public Works and the Department of Fisheries by the Tracadie board of trade urging the opening of the main Tracadie gully and protecting it by adequate breakwaters, so as to provide the Tracadie fishermen with a navigable outlet to the gulf of St. Lawrence fishing banks. This important undertaking, were it properly carried out along the lines suggested by the Tracadie board of trade, would provide Tracadie with its own fishing fleet and would undoubtedly mean the opening in the very near future of a large fish processing plant in that thriving village. As yet nothing is being done by our federal government.
Last summer I witnessed a spectacle which I would have liked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and the Minister of Fisheries to view for themselves. I happened to be at Miscou Point one afternoon as the fishermen were hauling their boats ashore. Hardship and brawn were the natural qualificatives which came to my mind as I watched these hardy Miscou fishermen straining, with the assistance of a homemade winch, to haul those heavy brine-soaked boats ashore. There is no wharf, no breakwater at Miscou Point. Yet within a few hundred yards from where I stood I was shown a spot locally known as Lake Fry which, with a little dredging, would provide a navigable entrance and thus afford a natural shelter at which the fleet could safely anchor. A somewhat similar situation obtains at Island River on Shippigan island, where lack of dredging deprives the local fishermen of another safe and natural haven for their boats.
Then if we proceed up shore we come to Maisonnette, another important fishing village of our county. There also we meet with another very discouraging situation for our fishermen because of the lack of a proper wharf at which to tie their numerous fishing boats safely. There is hardly one storm of any consequence in which several of their boats are not seriously damaged on the shore. Is it any wonder that, with local situations

The Address-Mr. Robichaud such as these prevailing in the best and most productive fishing county of New Brunswick, our boys abandon our fishing villages to seek an easier life somewhere else?
We all deplore the exodus of our young boys from the farms of Gloucester county. In so far as agriculture is concerned, we are passing through a real crisis. There are far too many abandoned farms in my county. A few years ago many of our good people raised their own vegetables, potatoes and turnips, grain and hay in sufficient quantities to feed their cows, hogs and hens, but now they go to the general store to purchase canned milk, potatoes, eggs and vegetables. This is a serious situation, and before long I fear we may experience the same slump in our fishing industry unless something is done by our federal government to encourage the sons of our fishermen to follow their fathers' calling and take to the open sea.
Another example of neglect on the part of our federal government is to be found in the village of Blue Cove. It is also an important and strategically located fishing centre. A number of companies consider Blue Cove as the real spot for the establishment of important fish processing plants. Along these shores herring and cod are especially plentiful. The lack of proper wharf facilities have so far prevented any major fishing development there. Oh, yes, Blue Cove has a wharf or breakwater. I do not know under what classification the Department of Public Works has listed the structure it erected at Blue Cove in 1929 or it might have been on the eve of the 1930 election, in apparent fulfilment of a promise made by Liberal politicians from time immemorial. It is quite a substantial structure, but it is not linked with the shore. By actual measurement the so-called Blue Cove wharf is exactly 750 feet from the shore at high tide, and 650 feet therefrom at low tide. Hon. gentlemen can realize the practical value of such a freak in public works. When you are on it, you need a boat to get ashore; and when fishing boats are moored thereto and a storm suddenly arises, you cannot reach this unfinished symphony, even with a boat, to salvage the fishing boats. I greatly doubt whether another such masterpiece exists in Canada, with the exception of course of Beresford, another fishing village in my own county of Gloucester where we were also gratified-by a Liberal administration, of course-with a similar anomaly of about the same vintage and uselessness as the Blue Cove wharf.
In order to bring these anomalies clearly to the attention of the Minister of Public


Works (Mr. Fournier) and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair)-because I do not expect the hon. gentleman will ever visit Blue Cove in the county of Gloucester-I have had enlargements made of photographs of the Blue Cove so-called wharf. I am sorry the Minister of Public Works is not here now because I wanted the permission of the Speaker to send the enlargements over to him, but I will do it later. I wish I could put them in Hansard, but unfortunately I cannot do so. I know that photographs are perfectly admissible in court as the best evidence. I therefore hope I am in order in sending them across the house to the Minister of Fisheries and to the Minister of Public Works. With these exhibits of best evidence in hand, surely the ministers will realize that it is high time the fishermen of Blue Cove and Beresford were given more humane and equitable treatment, and that those two unfinished, useless and costly structures were linked with the shore, as I hope they soon will be.

These are but a few of the most pressing needs of the fishermen of my constituency. It is not my intention, nor will time permit me today, to catalogue all the undertakings which the county of Gloucester deserves and expects from the federal Department of Public Works. Gloucester county has been the orphan child of the present federal administration. This is precisely one of the main reasons why our people indicated, by their votes at the May by-election, that it was time for a change- not the change advocated on Friday, I think it was, by the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis), but a real change this time. There was then, and still is, in this large county of ours which stands as the headpiece of the province of New Brunswick, between the mighty waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence on one side and the majesty of the baie de Chaleur on the other, a prevailing strong current of public opinion opposed to the present federal government because we have not received our just share in the distribution of public moneys. I was elected to the House of Commons in order that the voice of Gloucester would once again be heard, to further the interests of my constituents, to make their needs known to the government, and to appeal for fair and equitable treatment for our large county of Gloucester.
Before concluding my remarks on the question of fisheries, may I again stress the necessity of providing fishermen with some form of remuneration for losses sustained through storms. I am informed that a plan is now under advisement by the Department of

Fisheries to establish a permanent program of insurance as well as loans-interest free, I hope-to storm-stricken fishermen. May I advocate the elaboration of a system following the broad outline of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which has proved to be highly beneficial to western farmers. I am also in favour of extending the plan now under study so as to embrace some kind of cheap contributory insurance not alone on the fishing equipment but on the lives of our fishermen as well. After all, there is in my submission no more hazardous occupation than that of those hardy and courageous toilers of the sea who risk everything and face the ever-recurring dangers of storm and sea in order to develop the fishing grounds of Canada's Atlantic and Pacific coasts, which are recognized as the richest in the world. Hence special consideration should be given by our government to the welfare of Canada's fishermen; and a protective scheme of assistance and insurance is indeed long past due.
In the course of my remarks I have endeavoured to state the position of the province of New Brunswick with reference to the proposed Yarmouth-Bar Harbor, Maine, ferry service. I have also stressed the detrimental effects of the loss of British markets for our unmanufactured wood. Several aspects of our Gloucester county fisheries have been underlined with a view to obtaining more protection and more encouragement for our fishermen.
Before concluding, may I express the hope that my observations will receive the consideration which the people of my native province of New Brunswick and my own constituents are justified in expecting from the departments concerned.

Be that as it may, I want to say a word about the charge which has been levelled at the Social Credit movement for some considerable time. It is a charge that has been levelled at us by writers and by some political observers to the effect that, in reality, we are Conservatives. I noticed that when the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis) spoke the other day he said something similar to that. Referring to the Social Crediters he said, as reported at page 178 of Hansard:
I was told that a large number of Social Credit supporters were only disguised Tories. That is not a good recommendation as far as I am concerned, and there is good proof of it. Considering the matter further, if we look at the new cabinet that has been formed in British Columbia we find many ministers who were at one time prominent members of the Conservative party, so if they are not disguised Tories they are at least converted Tories.
That was said in this House of Commons. I am reminded that the hon. member who said this, while he now sits on the other side of the house, sat behind us when he first came here. Perhaps there is a measure of conversion there.
We have heard observations here and there about this same matter. Very often when newspaper writers are commenting on the record of the Alberta government they like to say that it is really a good, honest Conservative government. What gives rise to that sort of opinion? I think perhaps there may be three main reasons, the first of which is that for the last 17 years, since Social Credit was first represented in the House

The Address-Mr. Hansell of Commons, we have been sitting in opposition with the Tory party in Canada. This is no indication that we are part and parcel of them, but the fact is that often opposition members applaud opposition members. It just seems to be the normal process. Very often amendments and motions of want of confidence are offered, and we vote with the Tories. Perhaps that has added a little fuel to the fire.
Then there is this further basis of comparison, in that we do feel that our relationship with the British commonwealth of nations is very important. Traditionally, of course, the Conservatives take that position. We, too, have tried to stress our absolute allegiance to the British crown. We have that feeling; we hold that belief, and we have not wavered when we have had to come to any decision affecting that loyalty. It may be that that, too, has been a factor of similarity from which people have drawn certain conclusions.
Then the third point, of course, is found in the recent political trends. I refer of course to the British Columbia election and the fact that Mr. Bennett, a one-time member of the Conservative party, came over to the Social Credit ranks, is now premier of the province and is evidently doing a good job. Because a thing of that kind happens is no reason for saying that Social Crediters are, in reality, nothing but Tories. Nothing could be farther from the truth. Let us look at this matter from a safe and sane standpoint. In the first place, while some more or less prominent Conservatives may have come over to our movement in British Columbia, several rather prominent Liberals have also come over to us.

I do not claim to be a prophet or the son of a prophet, but I ask you to look at what happened in Great Britain. Just reminisce for a while. Years ago when I was a boy the two great parties in Great Britain were the

The Address-Mr. Hansell Liberals and the Conservatives. Well, what happened in the process of time? Labour came into the picture with a fairly strong leadership. Their ideas, which embraced certain tenets of socialism, came into the picture. They began to emerge and became stronger until Labour took over the government. My main purpose in rising this evening is to draw to the attention of this house some of the problems of my constituents. I do so because I sincerely believe that other constituencies in Canada are concerned with the same problems. I welcome the opportunity to discuss the speech from the throne, and desire particularly to refer briefly to one paragraph because I believe Canadians should be interested in it. The paragraph reads:
You will be invited to consider a measure to provide for federal co-operation with the provincial governments in the conservation of the water resources of Canada.
I am sure every right-thinking Canadian will welcome this legislation. I am hopeful also that each and every one of the provincial governments will take steps to provide the legislation, the administrative organization and the educational services necessary for the effective conservation of the water resources. In 1949, without a dissenting voice, the forestry act became law, thus opening the door to federal-provincial teamwork. I hope the same thing will happen in connection with this legislation.
The conservation of our natural resources is actually a problem of prime importance. The conservation of our forests, of our soil, of our water and the preservation of our wildlife are matters of grave concern to every Canadian. The conservation of water is of paramount importance, and it bears a close relationship to the conservation of our forests and our agricultural land. Floods and the shortage of water are too often considered by the public only from the standpoint of immediate inconvenience. Much more publicity will have to reach the public. Hard campaigning for conservation has been carried out by the Canadian Forestry Association and L'Association Forestiere Quebecoise. Both devoted the main part of their revenues to bringing home to the public, through their

magazines and other publications, the idea of conservation. For this reason they must command greater financial support from all governments, especially from the federal government.
At this point, 1 should like to congratulate the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) for having provided larger grants to the Canadian Forestry Association during the last two years. I hope the minister will see his way clear to recommending to the government that a substantial amount be granted to L'Association Forestiere Que-becoise. It has been wisely stated that the wealth and health of this world lies in the top six inches of its surface. The conservation of these top six inches is a problem of paramount importance to every nation, in order that its people may be well nourished and survive. If we do everything we can towards the conservation of our forests, our soil and our water, it will be easy to preserve that top six inches for our own good and for the welfare of our children.
There is another paragraph, Mr. Speaker, in the speech from the throne which to my mind is of great importance to all Canadians. This paragraph reads:
To give effect to recommendations made by the standing committee on banking and commerce at the last session of parliament and to extend its scope your approval will be sought for an amendment to the National Housing Act.
I do not intend to elaborate on this subject, but I hope we will do everything we can to provide all Canadians with adequate housing. I wish to congratulate the government for what it has done in the past; the undertaking was far-reaching and the results have been substantial.
Many other measures will be brought before this house. When they come before us we shall consider them calmly, laying aside and sacrificing if necessary our own interests and ambitions to think only of the interests of Canada and Canadians. Hon. members are aware of the importance of Canadian mining. It is already a great industry, and the future is even more impressive. A new record of production will be attained this year, if not in value at least in volume. Canada occupies first place in world production of asbestos, nickel and platinum. Canada occupies second place in world production of aluminum, cadmium, gold and zinc. It is third in the production of silver, fourth in cobalt, copper

Every new mine adds to the richness of Canada and of Canadians. The past was great but the future will be greater.
Is Canadian mining going to continue to forge ahead? Will the value of our mineral industry move upward to the $2 billion mark in the near future? In both cases I hope the answer is yes. However, this objective cannot be accomplished without careful planning. We shall need a large amount of risk capital. Our leading operators, our engineers and our miners have, in the past, shown that they were equal to the task. We shall need more of their kind. Over and above that, we shall need people who are imbued with the spirit of determination and perseverance, people who have the vocation of pioneers. We shall need people of the same calibre as those who in the past took up the challenge and met it successfully, thus rewarding Canada with tremendous advantages which are felt in every home in this country.
The Cambrian shield, this V-shaped area covering more than half of Canada, has not yet yielded its full measure of usefulness to Canada and to Canadians. This great storehouse retains untold treasures yet to be found. The success of the past is merely an indication of what may be found in the future.

The Address-Mr. Dumas
The mining industry means the steady creation of new wealth for the people of Canada. The earth's most essential minerals are of greatest importance to the entire civilized world. From Newfoundland to British Columbia the industry gives employment to more than 110,000 men. These men are the breadwinners of their families, and counting them with others who are supported directly by mining and who are living in Canadian mining communities, we have a population of over 500,000 people.
Mining communities may seem to bear little relation to the prosperity of eastern and western farmers, but let me say this, Mr. Speaker: 500,000 people represent a large number of mouths to feed and a large number of people to clothe and shelter. Statistics are available to prove that these mining centres buy more than $65 million worth of food each year from the Canadian farmers. What do the mining communities mean to the manufacturing and lumbering industries? The answer is this. Annually the mining communities are buying more than $150 million worth of clothing, shelter, furniture and other articles, and the same communities are buying each year more than $100 million worth of lumber, machinery, electrical equipment and other similar products.
Keeping in mind what I have just said, we will have a look at the gold mining industry and briefly analyse what it means to the economy of this country. Every day close to 50,000 tons of ore-bearing gold, silver and other minerals worth close to half a million dollars are passing through the 59 mills operated by the Canadian gold mines. Every working day close to 22,000 men, the breadwinners of a population of some 130,000 people, are employed in these mines.
There are 30 Canadian gold mining communities and they buy more than $12 million worth of food from Canadian farmers and more than $50 million worth of other services from the manufacturing and the lumbering industries. Each year the gold mines themselves are paying over $70 million in wages and more than $45 million in purchases of all kinds.
Surely an industry such as this must be considered to be of primary importance. I am sure hon. members will agree that an industry which has played so great a part in opening up northern Canada and in building up our national economy must be a matter of interest and concern to all Canadians. History may repeat itself and the gold mining industry may be called upon again-if not this time to save the country from bankruptcy, as it did before-at least to strengthen our national credit.

The gold mining industry is going through a difficult period because the official price set for the precious metal is much too low. Were it not for the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act few gold mines would still be operating. This legislation really rescued the declining industry. Many producers owe their continued operation to this assistance. The gold mining communities have also greatly benefited by it. The facts show that the legislation enacted by the government has done a real job. Proposed amendments to the act were outlined in a statement made last week by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and they will surely be of great help in assisting the industry to survive.
In this respect, I should like to quote an article which appeared under the title "Help For Gold Mines" in the Ottawa Journal of November 26, 1952:
More aid for marginal gold mines, beginning with 1953, should be welcomed by more than gold miners and owners of gold shares. Gold mining is one of the important industries of this country, supporting many communities, providing work and wages for scores of thousands, providing a profitable market for many allied industries, and undoubtedly a major factor in taking care of our international balances.
During recent years gold mining has suffered grievously through the fact that while operators of the mines have had to meet soaring costs in wages and other needs the world price of gold has remained at a fixed official level.
The help now provided by the government may not meet this situation entirely (the formula of assistance is so complicated a layman cannot understand it) but it is bound to make some difference, and in some instances, the Journal is informed by mining men, may make a substantial difference.
The only question that may be fairly asked is: In the light of knowledge by everybody that gold mining has been in jeopardy these past three years, why was this aid not given before?
While the article is good, I think the last paragraph is superfluous. The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was instituted at the beginning of 1948. It has been amended and extended, and has been profitable to the great majority of gold mines.
Many other newspapers had articles commenting favourably upon the proposed amendments to the assistance act. I should like to quote from a letter I received yesterday. It is dated November 28, 1952, addressed to myself, and states:
Our association wishes to go on record as commending heartily the recent amendment to the gold mines assistance act, under which additional costaid has been provided for the hard-pressed gold producers of the country.
Yours very truly,
Prospectors & Developers Association V. R. MacMillan President.

I have received many similar letters from people closely connected with the industry. They are all thankful for what is being done by the government to provide additional assistance to the gold mines.
Altogether there is ample evidence that this government is doing much to help the industry. The welfare of the gold mining communities has always been regarded by the government as of very great importance. For this I wish to express my thanks. The fact that the government has definitely stated that increased assistance will be provided is encouraging to the industry and to the residents of the gold mining communities. We are all very thankful.
No government would have made this effort and gone to this expense unless it was firmly convinced that the price of gold was much too low, and unless it had in mind that the situation was indeed a temporary one, that it should be corrected or that it would in time correct itself.
We must not forget this. We are sellers of gold, so we can hardly dictate the price to the buyers. We are not the largest producers, and for this reason we can only more or less influence the market. And, last but not least, the production and sale of gold is very important to our economy. I firmly believe that better days are not too far ahead for the gold mining industry. The future of gold is much better than some of us are inclined to think. I saw in this morning's press that Canada intends to support South Africa's request for a higher price for gold. I congratulate the Canadian government on this logical attitude, and for two reasons. The first is that this is the best way I know of to help the sterling bloc to get back on its feet. The second reason is that it will also be of great assistance to our people generally, and to the gold mines in particular.
There are two ways of helping the other commonwealth countries. The first is to give or lend them billions of dollars which either we will have lost or they will have to repay. The second is to do something that will be beneficial to all of us. In supporting South Africa we will be choosing the second method, which will be the most beneficial to all of us. I believe the choice is obvious.
When the price of gold is where it should be, the industry will take its rightful place in our economy. Instead of being a burden to the taxpayers of this country it will, as it did in the past, contribute generously to the welfare of Canada and its people. For the benefit of those who are afraid that the government is not doing the right thing, or that it is doing too much for the gold mines,
The Address-Mr. Fulford I should like to quote a short article from the Rouyn-Noranda Press of November 20, 1952. It states:
In terms of Canada's total budget gold assistance payments are not large. They are not large when compared to the sums paid out to carry other key industries, notably wheat growing, through bad times. They are not large when set against the revenues the federal government derives in corporation and personal income taxes from the industry and those who work in it.
I will ask those who are worried over this question to think twice before objecting to this increased assistance to an industry which needs it so badly. I will repeat what I said at the outset: Let us consider this question calmly, laying aside and, if necessary, sacrificing our personal interests and ambitions, to think only of the betterment of the nation as a whole, which demands everywhere and always that citizens shall be happy and contented with their lot.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on the speech from the throne one usually performs the perfunctory duty of complimenting the mover and seconder of the address in response to the speech from the throne. In this instance it is no perfunctory duty; it is a genuine pleasure. I can say without hesitation that in my view the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Deslieres) as mover and the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) as seconder made the best speeches I have heard on any parallel occasion during the years I have sat in the House of Commons. Certainly their speeches have put to shame many of the more futile efforts of those of us who have sat in the chamber a much longer time.
It was most gratifying to hear in the speech from the throne mention of the findings of the international joint commission in relation to the St. Lawrence seaway.
Recently I had the privilege of addressing a group of citizens of Canton, New York, in a large auditorium which had recently been opened at St. Lawrence university. I tried to deal with this matter from a different angle than is generally used. I did a little research, particularly on the subject of navigational facilities between the great lakes and the sea. I had said that all my life I had heard this referred to as the St. Lawrence deep waterway, and latterly as the St. Lawrence seaway and power development. I found that I spoke better than I knew because the first committee to advance the project was founded in 1902, and that happens to be the very year I was born.
As one delves into the history of the navigational facilities connecting the lakes and the ocean he will be interested to note that

The Address-Mr. Fulford from the beginning Canada has taken the initiative. The first connecting link was around the Lachine rapids and was constructed by the Capuchin Fathers in 1700. Naturally it was only a narrow ditch capable of carrying canoes loaded with furs. Then in 1797 the Northwest Fur Company, a private company, constructed a canal connecting lake Superior with lake Huron. This canal served a most useful purpose for fifteen years, but was completely destroyed by the United States army in the war of 1812.
I shall not bore the house with all the details of this history but shall try to say enough to demonstrate how proud we Canadians ought to be of the work we have undertaken. In the 1820's a private company began and completed a canal connecting lake Erie with lake Ontario. That was no small feat in those days when it is considered that the height of Niagara falls and the drop of the Niagara river had to be taken into account when the canal and locks were built. Later on this canal was taken over by the government of Upper Canada. Previous to that the government of Lower Canada had circumvented the stretch of river between Beau-harnois and lake St. Francis. Strangely enough the canal of that day followed closely what is now the Beauharnois canal.
It was not until many years later that the present Soulanges canal, which is used at present for navigational purposes, was built. Then in the 1840's the government of Upper Canada started and completed in stages the Cornwall canal and the Williamsburg canal. Those were finally completed in 1848 and permitted small draught vessels to ply between the upper great lakes and the St. Lawrence river below Montreal.
With the completion of the great Welland canal ships with a draught of 27 feet could be accommodated and the "only real bottleneck that exists today is the area from just above Cornwall, Ontario, down to the foot of the Lachine canal. There would be no restrictions upon Canada building a deep waterway in its entirety, as this section would be entirely within Canadian territory.
The section about which we would have to negotiate with the United States begins just above Cornwall and continues to a point just above Cardinal. This is the international section which will have to be developed jointly. Canada can go ahead with the navigational section and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has said that Canada courageously will go ahead. But we must have the co-operation of the United States in order to develop power.
We all know that the Canadian power will be developed by the Hydro Electric Power


Commission of Ontario. The international joint commission has given the green light to go ahead, but the matter is still being held up because of uncertainty in the United States as to which authority in the state of New York will be given the right to develop power, whether a federal power authority or a New York state power authority.
In the report of the international joint commission reference was made to the Gut dam; I trust you will not call me to order when I say "Gut dam". The Gut dam was built by Canada at a point between Prescott and Cardinal in order to divert water flowing between two islands to the head of the Cardinal canal and thus eliminate certain dangerously swift currents, and at the same time create a somewhat safer channel. I understand that engineers have estimated that this dam makes as much as eight inches difference in the water level of the upper reaches of the St. Lawrence river, with a somewhat lesser effect in lake Ontario. Not being an engineer I cannot give an expert opinion, but I venture to say that it does not make half an inch difference. I base that statement upon evidence I heard last summer at a hearing of the international joint commission at Ogdensburg, New York. At that time the treasurer of the Ogdensburg Trust Company stated that he owned land on the United States side both below and above the dam and he found that the height of water on both sides of the dam was exactly the same. In other words the water below the dam on the United States side was as high as the water above the dam. We who live in that part of the country know that on the United States side the dam is not visible. The shore line simply seems to be a continuation of the New York state side of the river. To me that evidence showed conclusively that the Gut dam made no difference. However, the international joint commission recommended that Canada should destroy this dam and work is now in progress to carry out that recommendation.
With Canada showing its good faith, I think it is only reasonable to ask our friends to the south to give proof of their good neighbour policy toward us by not holding up any longer than is necessary the action that will determine which body will be given the authority to proceed with the development of the power, whether it be the federal power authority or the New York state power authority. I am sure that every one of us in this house was most alarmed when we read last week in the press of Canada that the whole project may be held up eighteen months or more while Washington decides which authority will be granted the right to develop the power. Surely it is not asking

too much of our great neighbours to the south to ask them to co-operate with us as we have co-operated with them by carrying out the order of the international joint commission.
I should like to suggest that along the connecting waters of the St. Lawrence seaway project certain of the larger ports be designated as harbours under the Canada Shipping Act. I make this suggestion so that these harbours will have the necessary authority to regulate the course and speed of vessels plying up and down the narrow channels. Naturally I have special reference to my own town of Brockville. Recently large ships, both domestic and foreign, have been increasing their speed and the wash from these ships is constituting a menace not only to small craft owners who leave their craft in their boathouses but also and particularly to people who are out on the water in small craft such as rowboats, boats with outboard motors or even canoes. Sometimes in recent years we have seen waves come in that would almost make one think they were rollers coming off a vast ocean.
It has been stated that some years ago when the port of Albany, New York, was opened as the head of the seaway from New York city up the Hudson river one of the large steamship lines proceeded to send an ocean vessel up to Albany. That was well before the war, and that particular line is still settling lawsuits for the damage that was done to small craft, docks, boathouses and other buildings along the Hudson river. Certainly we do not want to see that happen when the St. Lawrence seaway is built. A certain amount of damage is being caused now, and I think it could be avoided if the necessary authority were given to the ports along the various streams connecting the great lakes and along the St. Lawrence connecting lake Ontario with the ocean.
The Address-Mr. Fulford
I also should like-and I have mentioned this in the house before-to call to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) the advisability of establishing a weather station somewhere along the upper reaches of the St. Lawrence river. At present the weather prophesying facilities in this district are unreliable. We do not have much fog in the Thousand Islands region but when we do they are bad fogs. Eventually a weather station will have to be set up somewhere between Cornwall and Kingston, and I should like to recommend that it be established as soon as possible. It must be done when navigation facilities for larger vessels are completed, and if it were done now it would be an invaluable aid to farmers in prophesying how severe a frost will be.
We are told to look at the Ottawa valley weather reports, that they will tell us what we can expect. That is not so, and I will give the house a concrete example. Last night, according to the official bulletins in the elevators in the parliament buildings, the temperature in Ottawa reached a minimum of 4 degrees above zero which would be more than enough to create a navigational hazard on the St. Lawrence. I understand that the lowest temperature reached in Brockville was 14 and that the lowest in Montreal was 13, which is not enough to cause a navigational hazard. Therefore in spite of the fact that Ottawa is so near the St. Lawrence valley the fact remains that we are in a different weather belt, and I believe our request for a weather station should be given consideration with the least possible delay.
